articles.title: ‘I am the code’: Trump clashed with ballroom architect over safety issues
articles.summary: In the weeks leading up to his resignation last year, the first architect on the White House ballroom clashed with President Donald Trump over design feature...
articles.body:
‘I am the code’: Trump clashed with ballroom architect over safety issues

In the weeks leading up to his resignation last year, the first architect on the White House ballroom clashed with President Donald Trump over design features that the architect believed violated building safety codes, according to two people with knowledge of the discussions and corroborating documents reviewed by The Washington Post.

James McCrery II withdrew from the project last October after warning repeatedly that Trump was insisting on a preliminary design that did not provide adequate emergency exit routes or fire-containment measures, said the people, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe the private discussions.

Trump brushed off McCrery's concerns, they said, and the president countered that no building codes apply to White House construction.

That episode, as described by the people familiar with the matter, offers new insight into Trump's priorities for the ballroom at a time when he is flexing executive power to fast-track construction projects across the nation's capital. The interviews and documents obtained by The Post - including early ballroom designs and images Trump appeared to have marked up with his trademark black-ink Sharpie - also show how deeply involved the president has been in the details of the project.

White House renovations and construction are typically handled by federal agencies required by law to comply with nationally recognized building safety standards to the "maximum extent feasible," unless doing so would present a national security risk.

But Trump's White House construction projects are being routed through the Executive Residence, a tiny office that is not a federal agency and is therefore exempt from rules governing agencies.

The District of Columbia government has no jurisdiction to enforce local building codes on federal property. The contractors hired to design and build the ballroom are responsible for adhering to safety standards as they work nearly round-the-clock to meet Trump's ambitious deadlines, according to experts.

Discussions about the life-safety deficiencies in the ballroom's design continued for months after McCrery resigned, according to White House records. It is not clear from the records reviewed by The Post whether the safety issues he identified have been resolved in more recent designs by Shalom Baranes Associates, the architecture firm that replaced McCrery's firm late last year.

Shalom Baranes Associates declined to comment.

When Post reporters visited McCrery's office this month, he asked them to leave and not contact him again. On Tuesday, in response to questions from The Post and details about its reporting for this story, McCrery issued a statement through a spokesman.

"President Trump entrusted me with the earliest stages of the new ballroom design," the statement said. "I am truly grateful for that honor and for the rich experience of working for him alongside all the highly talented and committed patriots at the Executive Mansion. Having completed the earliest designs, I stepped aside and a new firm was engaged."

The Post previously reported that McCrery clashed with Trump over the size of the ballroom. In response to questions Tuesday, McCrery did not provide a specific reason for his resignation. A White House spokesman emailed a statement that said it would be "factually false and totally inaccurate" to say that "McCrery's departure from the project was in any way associated with code issues."

Compliance with safety codes has been a priority since the East Wing project began, and aesthetics have not outweighed fire and safety standards, the statement said. The current team of architects and consultants is responsible for designing the East Wing according to nationally recognized fire and safety codes, it said.

"Life safety issues have been addressed and resolved continuously as the design has evolved," the statement said.

"McCrery was a valued member of the initial design team of the East Wing Modernization Project," the statement said. "The decision was made to move in another direction for the second phase of the project and we continue to make tremendous strides in realizing the goal of providing a world class military and functional facility for future Presidents to utilize."

The ballroom is the most expensive of the projects Trump has initiated to leave his imprint on monumental D.C. The president has described the project as a "gift" to the American people. Polls show that it is deeply unpopular. The Post previously reported that as of March, the ballroom project was expected to cost hundreds of millions more than the administration has publicly acknowledged - and that half the cost was expected to be covered by taxpayers.

Renderings show an ornate and gilded interior that departs from the simplicity of the original White House and echoes the look of the ballroom at Trump's Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida, a look he has said was inspired by the Palace of Versailles in France. A March budget for the new White House ballroom included nearly $6 million in gold leaf. The project also includes secure underground facilities that Trump has said are necessary for national security.

McCrery, a classical architect and professor at Catholic University of America, runs a boutique firm on Capitol Hill that specializes in designing churches, libraries and buildings for college campuses.

During his first term, Trump appointed McCrery to the United States Commission of Fine Arts, a position in which the architect consulted on projects in the capital through President Joe Biden's administration.

Trump handpicked McCrery Architects to design the aboveground portion of the ballroom, and the firm began drafting drawings as early as April 2025, documents show. "I am honored that President Trump has entrusted me to help bring this beautiful and necessary renovation to The People's House, while preserving the elegance of its classical design and historical importance," McCrery said in a White House news release announcing the project.

Trump was immersed in the minutiae of the project that spring and summer, often spending hours at a time discussing it at the White House with McCrery, the people with knowledge of the meetings said. The president also called McCrery on his cellphone at all hours to relay his thoughts on the design, they said.

The Post reviewed draft plans and other images featuring dozens of undated handwritten notes that appeared to be from Trump to McCrery as the two worked together on early designs for the ballroom. The notes were later returned to the White House, where images show they were stored in a box containing the label "Docs bearing POTUS's mark."

Sharpie markings on one of the documents expanded the footprint of McCrery's sketch of a ballroom that would have seated 640 guests. The Sharpie marks also scratched out proposed service corridors, extending the ballroom the entire width of the second floor.

The markings offer input on tiny details in the design, including how far decorative interior columns should extend into the ballroom or whether doors should hinge on the left or right. They emphasize a preference for Corinthian-style columns over simpler columns. And they cross out two sets of service stairs.

The documents reviewed by The Post also hint at friction, previously reported by The Post and others, that grew last summer as Trump insisted on expanding the ballroom until it was nearly twice the size of the historical mansion - a size that would seat more than 1,300 guests.

One document features an image of a planned data center overlaid on a map of Manhattan, a mash-up that demonstrated the data center's massive size. "James," begins a note for McCrery at the top, an apparent reference to the architect's concerns about the size of the ballroom, "And you think we are big."

Trump's growing vision for the ballroom triggered a cascade of design issues, including conflicts with building standards McCrery was trained to follow, according to the people familiar with their discussions.

McCrery informed the White House that Trump's ballroom design did not meet fire safety codes, which require the majority of guests to be able to quickly exit through the main entrance during an emergency, according to the people and documents. The architect also pointed out that alternative emergency exit routes out of the building were insufficient, and that there was little in the design to prevent a kitchen fire from rapidly spreading into the event space on the floor above.

In addition to fire safety concerns, Trump's desired ballroom design did not include enough toilets to accommodate the structure's maximum occupancy, according to documents, and there were few options for adding more, as the event space occupied most of the building's footprint. One early ballroom design featured just seven stalls in the women's bathroom.

On Sept. 30, 2025, a White House team met to review the ballroom design, and they discussed "areas of concern" and comments from contractors on the project, according to a White House official's meeting notes. "Life safety - big concern," the notes said.

Major renovations and construction on the White House are supposed to be handled by the General Services Administration or the National Park Service, according to a memorandum of understanding governing site operations.

The GSA, which handles most nonmilitary government real estate projects, has previously told The Post that it has no role in the ballroom project and Tuesday referred questions to the White House. The Park Service is acting as a pass-through for private donations to the project but is not running the construction. The Park Service did not respond to a request for comment.

Instead, the work has been routed through the White House Executive Residence, an unusual arrangement that has allowed the president to dictate the terms of the project, The Post previously has reported.

Typically, the GSA and other federal agencies write language into their construction contracts that allows them to enforce code compliance, according to Kevin Kampschroer, who oversaw numerous federal construction projects in a 50-year career at the GSA.

While it's difficult to quantify the risk of designing a structure without adequate emergency exits and other fire-protection mechanisms, Kampschroer said, "bottom line is, I don't know any commercial building owner that would cheat on the fire code, because the risk is too great."

The Post has not reviewed McCrery's contract with the White House but has examined the contract between the White House and the project builder, Clark Construction. The agreement says Clark must conduct its work in accordance with "Federal, State, and local laws, regulations, codes, directives, or guidance provided by the Contracting Officer." The contracting officer in this case is Joshua Fisher, director of White House management and administration and an assistant to Trump.

Fisher did not respond to a request for comment.

Clark has hired a private company to do third-party inspection of the construction, according to a memo notifying the White House of its plan to issue a no-bid subcontract for the work.

A spokesperson for Clark Construction, the project's general contractor, said in a statement, "As demonstrated by our successful history delivering projects for Federal clients across the United States, we consistently follow applicable building codes and life safety requirements."

Documents show that McCrery resigned the week of Oct. 20, the same week demolition began on the former East Wing.

In the months that followed his resignation, documents show, the White House team continued to discuss life-safety issues and a code review for the ballroom project. It is unclear if a review was ever completed.

"Life safety - needs POTUS buy in," read one White House official's notes from a Nov. 6 meeting on the project.

The ballroom plans should have been finalized by early June 2026, according to an initial schedule reviewed by The Post, but current and former administration officials - who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe private conversations - told The Post in late August that the president was still tweaking the design as construction continued.

"Refinements to the design are continuing as construction proceeds," said the White House statement to The Post. "These refinements are primarily associated with the interiors."

articles.title: New campaign aims to help millions at risk of losing Medicaid coverage under work requirements
articles.summary: On Jan. 1, new federal work and reporting requirements kick in for Medicaid, leaving millions at risk of losing healthcare coverage as states scramble to prepare for the most substantial change to the program in decades.
articles.body: MECHANICSVILLE, Va. — In 100 days, on Jan. 1, new federal work and reporting requirements kick in for Medicaid recipients, leaving roughly 10 million Americans at risk of losing healthcare coverage, as states scramble to prepare for the most substantial change to the program in decades. A new, $2 million campaign called “Keep Your Care,” an independent nonprofit, launched Wednesday. Shared exclusively with NBC News, it aims to educate states and Medicaid recipients ahead of the massive change. For Melanie and Greg Stephens, who live in a small town outside of Richmond, Virginia, the resources can’t come soon enough. On Aug. 31, the family received a letter in the mail informing them of the new guidelines. “When I received the letter about all the changes coming up, I had a panic attack because I was like, ‘Oh, my gosh, what does this mean?’” Melanie Stephens said. As full-time caregivers for their disabled daughter, Rachel, they are exempt from the 80-hours-per-month work or community service requirement that will affect most eligible adults in the new year. But they will still need to prove they are exempt every six months. “Our concern is not so much on our part because we are thorough,” Greg Stephens said. “Once it leaves us and goes to a Medicaid worker to process, that’s where we are concerned they’re going to miss a deadline or fall through the cracks, and we have no control over that.” The work requirements, supported by Republicans to address wasteful spending, were passed as part of the “big, beautiful bill” signed into law by President Donald Trump last year. But they could leave eligible recipients without coverage because of the administrative hoops they will now have to jump through, health care advocates argue. Virginia Health Secretary Marvin Figueroa, in an interview with NBC News, described it as “fighting government for something that you’re entitled to.” “I go back to just look at the debate that allowed this bill to pass. This is a predictable surprise,” he added. “The discussion was about losing coverage, and I think we’re going to see that across the board.” Senate Majority Leader John Thune and many Republicans defended the cuts at the time, arguing they were “targeting waste, fraud, and abuse in the program” and also “want to make sure that this doesn’t hurt beneficiaries.” “And what’s being said out there by the Democrats is totally inaccurate,” Thune said in an interview last year, days before his chamber voted to pass the legislation. “It doesn’t cut Medicaid … What we’re talking about here is getting rid of waste, fraud and abuse, strengthening and improving the program for the people who need it the most and for whom it was intended, and really making this program more solvent for the long term.” Keep Your Care was established by two health care advocacy groups, Caring Across Generations and the Healthcare Education Project, and the Service Employees International Union. The group’s state-level work will focus on Georgia, North Carolina, Illinois, Michigan, California, Virginia and New York, states with Medicaid expansion under the Affordable Care Act where millions stand to lose coverage. The group is working with communities to help eligible Americans maintain coverage, and influence state and local governments on how the new requirements are implemented. Its website will list state-specific information about what is changing, determine the requirements and exemptions that may apply and track reporting deadlines. Greg Stephens admitted that, as a physician, he judged patients who were covered by Medicaid until he became a recipient himself. But his daughter Rachel, 22, has faced increasing health challenges since Covid and requires 24/7 management: so much so that he quit his job last year, just as his wife had years before. With no income on paper, they had to apply for Medicaid. “We spent months calling other insurance companies and other agents and trying to find another way, and there was no other way,” Melanie Stephens shared during an interview at their home, accomplished because Rachel’s grandparents looked after her during the 30-minute window. The coverage allows the Stephens to care for Rachel, who is bound to a wheelchair, at home, which also means administering medications five times per day and feeding her through a tube. Rachel’s care is so complex that the only other option for their daughter, the Stephens said, would be an institution. “There’s no one that could possibly care for her medically, or emotionally or cognitively,” the Stephens shared, adding: “She would have no will to live.” The Stephens acknowledged that while there may be some individuals on Medicaid who could work, the changes made were an overcorrection, burdening eligible families with unnecessary stress and paperwork. “There’s a lot of people that are getting health care through Medicaid expansion, like ourselves, that absolutely need this exclusion to be able to do what we do,” Greg Stephens said.

articles.title: EXCLUSIVE: Ossoff challenged to return Epstein-linked donation or retract ‘Epstein class’ attack
articles.summary: Democrat Sen. Jon Ossoff faces calls to return a $7,000 donation from Reid Hoffman, a billionaire who admitted visiting Jeffrey Epstein's island.
articles.body: EXCLUSIVE: Democrat Sen. Jon Ossoff of Georgia is being criticized as a "hypocrite" and faces a challenge to return a sizable donation from a Jeffrey Epstein-linked billionaire or drop one of his main lines of attack on Republicans as representing the "Epstein class." Ossoff has framed his re-election effort as pushing back on the influence of wealthy elites and getting big money out of politics. However, his campaign received the maximum legal contribution of $7,000 from Silicon Valley billionaire Reid Hoffman, a venture capitalist who previously admitted to visiting Epstein’s private island. Hoffman also donated $1 million to an Ossoff-linked political action committee, New Engagement PAC. Hoffman has not been accused of any wrongdoing. But Ossoff’s Republican challenger, Rep. Mike Collins, says that accepting donations from Hoffman shows Ossoff "has been nothing but a hypocrite the entire time." In an interview with Fox News Digital, Collins said he is giving Ossoff a very simple choice: return the Reid Hoffman donation or explain why the "Epstein class" does not include one of his own maximum-dollar donors. DEM ‘EPSTEIN CLASS’ ATTACK BACKFIRES AS TOP CANDIDATES FUNDED BY EPSTEIN-TIED BILLIONAIRE On the campaign trail, Ossoff has railed against American politics for "running on secret money, corporate money, billionaire money" and accused the Trump administration of taking "American corruption to spectacular new heights." He released a statement earlier this year, saying, "We were told that MAGA was for working-class Americans. But this is a government of, by, and for the ultra-rich... this is the Epstein class, ruling our country. They are the elites they pretend to hate." However, one of Ossoff’s donors, Hoffman, a Seattle-based billionaire, has previously admitted to spending a night on Epstein’s Caribbean island. Their first known meeting was on July 19, 2013, almost five years after Epstein pleaded guilty in Florida to state charges of soliciting prostitution and procuring a minor for prostitution. According to Massachusetts Institute of Technology records, Hoffman, then a member of the university’s Media Lab Advisory Council, met with Epstein alongside other faculty members on campus. The next year, Hoffman visited Epstein’s private island, Little Saint James, and stayed overnight, The Wall Street Journal reported. Business Insider reported that in a recent podcast appearance, Hoffman admitted to staying one night at Epstein’s island as part of an MIT fundraising trip. Regarding his visit, he quipped, "Note to self: Google before going." The Wall Street Journal reported that later in 2014, Hoffman sent Epstein ice cream, writing that it was for him or "for the girls." Hoffman has since apologized for his association with Epstein, saying that "by agreeing to participate in any fundraising activity where Epstein was present, I helped to repair his reputation and perpetuate injustice. For this, I am deeply regretful." DEMS DESCEND ON POSH ISLAND GETAWAY PACKED WITH DEEP-POCKETED DONORS AS MIDTERMS CLOSE IN This election cycle, Hoffman donated $7,000 to Ossoff’s campaign. In August, Hoffman also donated $1 million to New Engagement PAC, a Georgia-based political organization run by former Ossoff senior advisor Alexander Edelman. New Engagement has spent nearly $500,000 on media opposing Collins, according to September FEC filings reviewed by Fox News Digital. Fox News Digital reached out to New Engagement PAC and Edelman for comment. Collins told Fox News Digital that Ossoff’s acceptance of Hoffman’s donations is "sending a plain and clear message to the voters of Georgia." "He doesn't care about our state; he doesn't represent the people of the state or the values of our state. If he did, he certainly wouldn't be associating himself with some of the Epstein friends out there, just taking money directly, maxed out, from Reid Hoffman who was in the Epstein files as an Epstein friend," he said. He noted, "I could see it now if somebody gave you 20 bucks, and you didn't know who it was, but when somebody maxes out to your campaign directly, you know who they are, but yet you still take it. And then you turn around, and you go out there like a hypocrite, and you talk about President Trump and the Epstein files when you, in fact, are tied to it." OBAMA STRATEGIST TURNS ON RISING DEM STAR OVER VIRAL TRUMP ATTACK: 'GRATUITOUS AND UNNECESSARY' Collins argued that Ossoff, widely considered a rising star in the Democratic Party, is actually using his Georgia Senate campaign as a launching pad for a future presidential run. "It's very clear that this guy is just using Georgia as a platform," he alleged. "He is going to get as much money as he can. He does not care where it comes from." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "So, we are here to condemn and demand that John Ossoff condemn Reid Hoffman, refund that donation, and tell Reid Hoffman we demand that you stop funding his campaign." SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Fox News Digital reached out to Hoffman through Greylock, a venture-capital firm at which he currently sits as a partner. Fox News Digital also reached out to Ossoff's campaign for comment.

articles.title: Zelenskyy to seek offramp for yearslong Russia war in UN speech after Trump reveals peace deal is close
articles.summary: Volodymyr Zelenskyy addresses the United Nations General Assembly with security proposals as Trump presses for a faster Russia Ukraine war deal.
articles.body: NEW YORK — Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is set to address the United Nations General Assembly Wednesday as President Donald Trump presses for an end to Russia’s war and Kyiv seeks to shape the emerging diplomatic push after more than four-and-a-half years of conflict. Zelenskyy’s speech comes the day after he met with Trump in New York, where the two discussed finally putting an end to the war. Trump said that he believes a deal can be reached, though he did not disclose what that agreement would involve. "We’re working very closely with the leaders of Russia and Ukraine, and we will get that one done," Trump said, adding that an agreement would happen "more quickly than people understand." KUSHNER, WITKOFF SET FOR KYIV TALKS AFTER PUTIN MEETING IN US PUSH FOR PEACE The Ukrainian president has said he is bringing "concrete security proposals and de-escalation measures" to New York for the annual United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) gathering. His government is also seeking additional air defenses, support for Ukraine’s energy infrastructure and help protecting food exports through the Black Sea. The meeting with Trump came as Russia and Ukraine appeared to be weighing a possible pause in attacks on energy infrastructure. Zelenskyy has said Russian strikes on Ukraine’s energy sector, critical infrastructure and food exports should stop, followed by matching de-escalation steps from Kyiv. UKRAINE SEEKS MORE US PATRIOT INTERCEPTORS AS BOMB SHELTER PROBE DEEPENS Trump has also urged Ukraine to halt its strikes on Russian oil refineries. Ahead of his meeting with Zelenskyy, he called the campaign "a serious hit against the Russians," but added, "It’s also a serious hit on the price of diesel." In his U.N. address on Tuesday, Trump said he could use new tariff authority against buyers of Russian energy "if necessary" to bring the war to an end. "This ridiculous and never-ending war with Ukraine must be ended. The whole world suffers as 25,000 people, mostly soldiers, are being killed each month. What a shame!" Trump said. The competing priorities are likely to shape the diplomatic conversation around Zelenskyy’s Wednesday appearance before UNGA — Trump is pressing for a faster path to negotiations, while Ukraine is seeking the military support and security commitments it says are necessary for any agreement to hold. The timing is especially consequential as winter approaches. U.N. investigators have warned that renewed Russian attacks on Ukraine’s power grid could leave millions without electricity or heat. Kyiv is seeking more Patriot air defense systems, energy assistance and support for efforts to produce U.S.-designed interceptors inside Ukraine. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Zelenskyy’s remarks could offer a clearer indication of how Kyiv views the next phase of the war, including what it expects from Washington, how much responsibility it wants Europe to assume and what conditions it would attach to any cease-fire or peace agreement.

articles.title: Welder turned lawmaker sees a ‘nuclear bomb for work’ — and a chance to help blue collar Americans
articles.summary: Rep. Riley Moore, a former welder, warns AI could be the "nuclear bomb" for blue-collar jobs or a force-multiplier for manufacturing workers.
articles.body: Before AI threatened to reshape the kind of blue-collar work he once did, Rep. Riley Moore was a welder on an Appalachian mining operation. Now, as the technology races into the workplace, Moore argues it could make workers like him safer and more productive rather than replace them. The West Virginia Republican has taken that message to the Teamsters and other labor stakeholders as Congress and businesses grapple with how quickly AI should reshape the workplace and how much of a role government should play amid economic and national security concerns. "I started my career off as a welder and I come from a blue-collar background, not just myself, my mother's family [were] all welders, actually. AI represents a massive potential for positive advancements in manufacturing. But it also represents potentially the nuclear bomb for work as we know it in the world," Moore said in an exclusive interview Monday with Fox News Digital. Representing a state still closely tied to mining and manufacturing, Moore has taken his message to the Teamsters and other labor stakeholders, arguing that AI should become a "force-multiplier" for workers rather than simply replace them. WATCH: AMERICANS WARN AI WILL TAKE JOBS DESPITE REASSURING LABOR DATA: ‘JUST WAIT’ Moore said he leans toward finding the "positives" in AI development and that, if the technology can complement blue-collar labor rather than replace it, it could be a game-changer for the U.S. economy and its workers. "I think AI certainly has the ability to extend the longevity of a worker in a particular trade. It can also make those jobs safer. It can extend the time period in which somebody can work without injury. And it can also create better efficiencies, which then can also better paying jobs here in this country." I FEARED AI WOULD LEAVE MY COMMUNITY BEHIND. NOW I SEE A PATH TO PROSPERITY "Or, it’s the nuclear weapon [against] work, it could potentially eliminate jobs as we know it and get rid of what is really critical, I think, to being a human being: which is human purpose, which work is certainly part of that and the dignity of work and contributing to civil society." Moore’s district includes major commercial arteries like Interstates 79 and 81 and the new Trans-Allegheny U.S. 48, which the lawmaker helped open this year. The trucking industry, historically unionized, could benefit from AI, he said, while warning that self-driving rigs could endanger the trade. "I'm against automated trucking, but I am in favor of having AI as part of trucking to make the road safer and keep that driver safer and make them more productive," he said, considering AI could act as a "co-pilot" to protect against drowsy driving or other dangers that come from being inherently human. The trucker would remain employed, and crash-prone 81 could become less so: "That creates the types of efficiencies that we're looking for, certainly, but then also respects the dignity of the human being and the worker who is involved in it." Religious leaders have expressed similar concerns about AI’s effect on the dignity of work. Pope Leo XIV’s May encyclical considered two biblical models for the AI era: "constructing the Tower of Babel" or following Nehemiah in rebuilding the walls of Jerusalem. "We certainly want to be Nehemiah," he said. Moore has also spoken with and met with the Teamsters as unions grapple with AI’s potential effect on their workers. A Teamsters spokesperson declined additional comment but praised Moore’s appearance at the event. Using AI to improve workflow efficiencies could raise wages, while U.S. leadership in AI could help counter China’s growing dominance in the AI "arms race." FETTERMAN ALIGNS WITH TRUMP ON AI PUSH, WARNS CHINA BENEFITS FROM US 'OVERREACTION' Data centers powering the technology have also become a point of controversy in Moore’s district and around the country. In the Eastern Panhandle, within 100 miles of Washington, D.C., and in the high-elevation forests of Tucker County farther west, residents and local leaders continue to debate the arrival of data centers that have already begun proliferating farther east. HOMEOWNERS IN THE HEART OF AMERICA’S AI BOOM ARE GETTING AN UNEXPECTED PAYOFF Moore said the three important questions are whether data centers will produce their own energy or rely on the local grid, whether they will siphon off public water or use "closed-circuit" cooling, and whether the community wants them there. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Fierce debate continues over whether tax revenue from the centers can be balanced with community concerns. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "I think as a Republican, we certainly believe in federalism and allow those communities to be able to have input of whether they're going to have a data center in their backyard or not," he said.

articles.title: Trump embraced a socialist he’s told voters to fear. Republicans aren’t thrilled
articles.summary: Trump praised Zohran Mamdani weeks after calling Democrats "communists," leaving GOP strategists frustrated ahead of the critical midterm election.
articles.body: Six weeks before the midterms, President Donald Trump is complicating one of Republicans' central campaign arguments against Democrats — warmly praising New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani after repeatedly warning voters about the rise of socialism and communism on the left. "I want him to be a great mayor, and he’s certainly got potential, got great potential," Trump told reporters as he patted Mamdani on the back after the two leaders met Monday at New York City's Gracie Mansion. The meeting, where the two leaders discussed cost of living and housing issues, isn't sitting well with some Republicans fighting to keep control of the House and Senate in the midterms. "All of it is self-inflicted, off-message, not helpful," a GOP strategist who asked to remain anonymous to speak freely told Fox News Digital. "None of these candidates out in these states, where these races are tighter and more competitive than they should be, are helped by any of this." MAMDANI TELLS TRUMP BANNED NEWS OUTLETS ARE WELCOME AT NYC MEETING Another Republican consultant, who also asked for anonymity, argued, "This is a president who is in a fully self-indulgent period. It doesn't seem like he really cares about winning. It's all off-key." Less than two weeks ago, Trump told Republicans gathered in Dallas at the GOP's first-ever midterm convention that there is a "communist" takeover of the Democratic Party. "In state after state, the Democrat establishment has been overthrown and replaced by crazed lunatics and radicals. They call themselves Democrat socialists, but actually, they’re communists," the president said. THE GOP'S 'SOCIALIST' MIDTERM PLAYBOOK Fast-forward to Monday, and Trump held his third meeting with Mamdani since he won election last year as the first socialist and first Muslim mayor of the nation's most populous city. A third GOP strategist, who was also granted anonymity, argued, "It seems he keeps on stepping on the message, making the election about how crazy the left is and communists and socialists and then appearing with them and yukking it up." A top Trump supporter quickly took to social media to blast the encounter. "I am a die hard Trump supporter and today I am feeling demoralized because Mamdani is a full blown communist jihadist. He is the spiritual leader of the communists in America and he met with the President today in NYC less than 45 days before the midterms," right-wing activist and MAGA champion Laura Loomer argued on social media. Loomer, an internet personality who has carved out an influential unofficial role as a Trump confidant, emphasized, "How is this supposed to make Trump’s most loyal supporters feel? We don’t feel very happy today. We were told to FIGHT communism. But when we fight communism, we see the communist get rewarded... The base is very angry today." DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB Alex Bruesewitz, a longtime Trump aide who now serves as a leading outside adviser to the president, shot back on X, writing, "I don’t understand the "Republicans" who are upset about the President having a friendly relationship with the Mayor of New York @ZohranKMamdani. It’s not wrong to have friendly relationships with people you disagree with. In fact, it’s healthy and good for you!" Republicans are fighting against traditional political headwinds facing the party in power and a rough political climate fueled by persistent inflation, surging gas and diesel prices, what polls show is a very unpopular war with Iran, and Trump's underwater approval ratings. To flip the script, a key part of the GOP playbook aims to turn what's normally a referendum on the party in power into a choice election by painting all Democrats on the ballot as far-left radicals. While some Republican strategists say Trump is stepping on the message, others are not concerned. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER "I don't think it's that big a deal," veteran GOP consultant Dave Carney told Fox News Digital. Carney said that Trump's meeting with Mamdani "goes with his role" as president, "and it's not a political role. The federal government and the president and the city have to work together." articles.title: Defending Trump media ban, DOJ cites national security and says White House access is a ‘privilege’
articles.summary: The Department of Justice said in a court filing late Tuesday that President Donald Trump has the right to ban media outlets CNN, MSNOW and Politico from the White House, calling their access a “privilege” and citing national security concerns.
articles.body: The Department of Justice said in a court filing late Tuesday that President Donald Trump has the right to ban media outlets CNN, MSNOW and Politico from the White House, calling their access a “privilege” and citing national security concerns. The filing urges a federal judge not to block the ban, ahead of a hearing Wednesday on the news organizations’ request for a temporary order restoring their access. The Trump administration argues that the ban does not violate First Amendment protections on press freedom. “Access to the White House is a privilege—not a right,” the DOJ says in the filing. It contends that the three news outlets had “failed to maintain basic minimum ‘standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House Complex,’ including, “publishing sensitive or classified information,” wrote DOJ Attorney Michael Velchik. The DOJ said the three news organizations were sent individual letters from the White House Press Office earlier Tuesday laying out the reasoning for the revocation of their passes, and citing a “non-exhaustive list of reporting incidents” the White House said it had found “threatened national security and spread falsehoods.” The letters cite stories on construction details related to the East Wing bunker, funding for the White House ballroom, munitions stockpiles impacted by the Iran war and sanctions against Russia. The outlets did not immediately respond to overnight requests for comment from NBC News on the filing’s claims. The letters give the news organizations a deadline of 5 p.m. on Friday to “contest this initial decision.” If the deadline is missed “this initial decision will be final,” they say. The decision to ban CNN, Politico and MS NOW came Friday via a Truth Social post, where Trump wrote that he was “proud to announce” the ban from the White House “effective immediately.” He said the decision was “a result of their constant “reporting” FAKE NEWS! Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America.” He added: “Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow.” Journalists from the three outlets, including MS NOW reporter Akayla Gardner, CNN’s Betsy Klein and Politico’s Cheyenne Haslett, subsequently found their access passes deactivated and their White House press credentials confiscated. First Amendment experts and the White House Correspondents’ Association called the turning away of credentialed reporters unconstitutional. CNN, Politico and MS NOW filed their lawsuit Monday arguing that the president’s move violated the defendants’ due process rights and First Amendment protections for newsgathering and speech. The three outlets said they were filing the lawsuit “to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes.” U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, who was appointed by Trump in 2017, will preside over the hearing Wednesday. He will evaluate the outlets’ request to issue a temporary restraining order blocking enforcement of the ban and restoring reporters’ hard passes to access White House grounds. Kelly ruled against Trump in a similar case back in 2018, when the White House withdrew credentials from reporter Jim Acosta, who was then with CNN. On Tuesday, Trump remarked that he would “probably” ​let journalists from CNN, ⁠MS ​NOW and ​Politico back into the White ​House if ​a court rules ‌against ⁠his decision to ban the ​media ​outlets ⁠from the White ​House grounds. Later that day, during his address to the United Nations’ General Assembly in New York, Trump told CNN reporter Kaitlan Collins: “You shouldn’t be here ... You said you weren’t going to cover me.” Collins responded that CNN never said it was not going to cover Trump, and that while it had been banned from the White House it was credentialed by the U.N. as usual. The solidarity among TV networks has been swift, as they refused to provide TV pool coverage of the president’s activities this week, resulting in quiet mics and a lack of photographs of Trump’s official activities. Pool coverage is when one network attends an event and then distributes information and media, such as video footage and audio, to other outlets. The system has been recognized by administrations from both parties for decades, and the coverage is used by pool members and subscribers, which includes outlets like Newsmax, One America News Network, C-SPAN and international outlets. Print and radio pools are still in place, and TV pools for events for other parts of the administration will continue. Individual TV networks, including NBC News, continue to provide coverage of White House events that are open to the press, outside of the pool. Outside of events, NBC News reporters continue to report on the administration’s activities.

articles.title: Trump meets US-backed Venezuelan president for first time since Maduro seized
articles.summary: Rodriguez was handpicked by Trump as leader of Venezuela was arrested and taken to the US
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump has held talks with Venezuela's interim President Delcy Rodríguez at the UN General Assembly, their first face-to-face meeting since the White House backed her to take over the South American country's government.

Rodríguez succeeded Nicolás Maduro shortly after US forces conducted a raid on the Venezuelan capital Caracas and seized him.

The pair met a few kilometres from the New York jail where Maduro is awaiting trial for drug trafficking and other charges.

Rodríguez said they discussed "advancing a cooperation agenda in strategic areas such as energy, mining, and security".

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles also attended the meeting.

Rodríguez's government has signed an agreement allowing the US to control more than 65 billion barrels of its oil - more than a fifth of the country's reserves. It grants a US-led company 100-year concessions over 17 oilfields in Venezuela.

Trump previously called it "the biggest oil deal in world history".

During his address to the UN on Monday, Trump said the US and Venezuela control "more than 60%" of the world's oil, adding: "To the victor belong the spoils."

Rodríguez is due to address the UN on Wednesday.

She previously served as vice-president to Maduro and was sanctioned by the US in 2018, but the measures were lifted in April this year.

She was sworn in as interim president by Venezuela's National Assembly days after the US raid with the White House's blessing.

Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado has repeatedly been barred from re-entering the country .

articles.title: Democrats in competitive races fight back against GOP’s communist labels
articles.summary: Democrats in tight Senate and House contests are fighting back against efforts to brand their party as communist, an effort they say has taken on new urgency in a midterm cycle that has seen candidates backed by the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) dominate in high-profile primary races. At the Republican midterm convention this month,…
articles.body:
Democrats in tight Senate and House contests are fighting back against efforts to brand their party as communist, an effort they say has taken on new urgency in a midterm cycle that has seen candidates backed by the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) dominate in high-profile primary races .

At the Republican midterm convention this month, GOP leaders warned of the dangers of a blue wave in November. President Trump said, “It’s going to be a communist country if they win,” while House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) claimed there was a “Bolshevik Revolution” going on in the Democratic Party.

“Next year the communists will be in Congress,” Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) said at the convention. “That’s what’s so frightening.”

There are no known congressional candidates who identify as communists, according to Joe Sims, co-chair of the Communist Party USA, but the recent wave of leftist primary wins has forced Democrats in competitive races to navigate efforts to tie them to the socialist wing of their party.

“The left says — not without reason — ‘They’re going to call us socialists no matter what,’” Matt Bennett, co-founder of the centrist think tank Third Way, told The Hill. “That’s true.”

“The problem is, you provide them with a lot more ammunition if you’ve got people who are actually socialists running and winning seats in Congress, and members of the DSA who are not just socialists but are supporting a platform that is completely bonkers,” Bennett continued.

Some Democrats in increasingly fierce contests are responding by drawing an explicit line between themselves and socialism.

In a recent ad in Kansas, Democratic Senate nominee Adam Hamilton took aim at the far left and his opponent, Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.), saying “both extremes just don’t get it” and “we have to fix our broken politics by meeting in the middle.”

“On one side, the far left pushes socialism and open borders,” Hamilton said in the ad. “On the other side, Roger Marshall gives us higher gas and grocery prices while slashing our healthcare. What’s going on in Washington? It’s just not who we are.”

In South Carolina, where Sen. Darline Graham (R) is seeking a full term after her summer appointment to fill her late brother’s seat, Democrat Annie Andrews is similarly trying to distance herself from the socialist label.

She released a recent ad in which she sits beside her Republican father, and text displayed over the video reads, “My dad voted for Lindsey Graham,” followed by an italicized quote that says “Annie’s not some crazy socialist!”

The push to draw a distinction extends beyond individual campaigns.

Reps. Tom Suozzi (N.Y.) and Adam Gray (Calif.), the only two Democrats to flip Trump-won districts in 2024, helped launch “Promise to America,” an initiative aimed at moving the party toward the center.

The group’s pledge — which begins by stating “We are capitalist, not socialist” — has since been signed by 10 members of Congress, 12 congressional candidates, about 60 state and local elected officials and roughly 1,000 grassroots activists, according to the group’s director, Felix Frisch.

Rep. Don Davis (D-N.C.) told The New York Times in an interview this month that he signed the letter because voters were expressing anxiety about communism.

“I have heard it from the northernmost portions of the district to the central all the way to the southernmost portions of eastern North Carolina,” he told the Times. “Without any doubt, yes, there are genuine concerns.”

Frisch said the effort is aimed at reaching voters who are dissatisfied with President Trump but remain wary of Democrats because they view the party as too far left.

“I think there are a lot of voters out there that are distrustful of Donald Trump — he has a very low approval rating — but are unwilling to make the jump to vote for Democrats, at least not yet, because they’re distrustful and worried about Democrats being extreme,” Frisch told The Hill.

Frisch argued that the prominence of DSA-backed candidates has also given an outsized impression of the left’s influence within the Democratic Party.

“Most Democrats that are out there right now are more moderate than the media wants them to believe,” he said. “They’re just not seeing that attention given to people who are running for office and embracing more pragmatic values.”

Megan Romer, the DSA’s co-chair, previously argued that the organization’s members are representative of the party’s base.

But polling paints a mixed picture of the ideological makeup of the Democratic Party. In a Pew Research Center survey this year, 39 percent of Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents put themselves at the party’s left, 36 percent put themselves at the party’s right, and 23 percent put themselves at the same ideological point as the party.

A separate New York Times/Siena University poll released last week suggests the socialist label could be problematic for Democrats among the broader electorate. The poll found 51 percent of likely voters viewed socialism unfavorably, compared with 31 percent who viewed it favorably. Thirty percent said they would be less likely to support a candidate who identified as a democratic socialist, while 13 percent said they would be more likely to do so, and 44 percent said it would make no difference.

Half of surveyed voters also described the Democratic Party as too far to the left, up from 47 percent earlier this year.

Earlier this month, eight House Democrats joined Republicans in voting for a resolution that condemned “socialism in all its forms,” including the Democratic Socialists of America. The resolution passed 220-192, with two Democrats voting present. It also called for passage of the GOP-backed election bill, the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (SAVE America) Act, which complicated the vote for some Democrats.

Rep. Josh Gottheimer (D-N.J.), who opposed the measure, sought consideration for an amendment that would have stripped out the election bill language but kept the condemnation of socialism. He criticized Republicans’ approach to the vote.

“If you really look at it, it’s just the SAVE Act with a wrapper on it,” Gottheimer told reporters earlier this month. “They’re not actually interested in getting people on the record on whether socialists are part of the Democratic Party.”

Republican strategist Ron Bonjean said the effort to paint Democrats as communists is helpful to the GOP, and the fact that moderate Democrats have pushed back on that effort forcefully “tells me everything.”

“It tells me the argument is working,” he said. “It tells me that Democrats are really worried about it because there is a split in the Democratic caucus, and that they’re worried about being defined, not just for this election, but for the long term, as socialists.”

“It could be a major issue in the 2028 election,” Bonjean added.

The attacks come as Republicans face broader political headwinds leading up to November. A Reuters/Ipsos poll released Monday put Trump’s approval rating at 32 percent, while Democrats held an 8-point advantage on the congressional ballot. And just 17 percent of survey respondents approved of Trump’s handling of the cost of living.

Still, Bennett said of the “communist” argument: “I do think it resonates, and I think they have to be worried about it.”

“I don’t think it’s going to work,” he said. “But I do think it gives them a lifeline in a moment where they don’t have another one.”

articles.title: Pete Hegseth confronts House with a lame-duck impeachment dilemma
articles.summary: The impeachment effort against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth posed a dilemma for Republican leaders ahead of the midterms. In the lame duck, it could be Democrats in the bind. Hegseth is leading an unpopular war in Iran, and GOP leaders were eager to avoid an impeachment vote this month, which would have put some vulnerable…
articles.body:
The impeachment effort against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth posed a dilemma for Republican leaders ahead of the midterms. In the lame duck, it could be Democrats in the bind.

Hegseth is leading an unpopular war in Iran, and GOP leaders were eager to avoid an impeachment vote this month, which would have put some vulnerable Republicans in a tough spot heading into November’s elections. Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) defused the issue by punting that vote until after the elections.

But the tides are likely to turn after the election, when Republicans will be freed to weigh in on Hegseth’s fate without fear of a voter backlash, while Democrats will face a tougher choice.

Do they go charging after Hegseth full bore, to appease a liberal base demanding Pentagon accountability? Or do they tread more cautiously, to allow time for the formal investigations many Democrats say they want to see before backing something as explosive as impeachment?

Rep. Jamie Raskin (Md.), the senior Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, which has jurisdiction over impeachment proceedings, suggested that answering those questions won’t be easy.

“I think that all impeachment articles should be sent to the Judiciary Committee, and we should scrutinize them,” Raskin, a former professor of constitutional law, said last week as Congress was leaving Washington for the long campaign recess.

“I’m not a huge fan of pop-up impeachments,” Raskin continued, “but if that’s all Speaker Johnson leaves us, then we will have to take it very seriously.”

The issue will be an early, postelection test for House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), who has walked a delicate line under President Trump’s second term as he vies to become the first Black Speaker in U.S. history.

On one hand, Jeffries has faced pressure from the left to fight the president tooth and nail at every turn, no matter the topic. On the other, Jeffries has sought to avoid alienating more moderate voters who are the key to winning battleground districts.

His decision will become even trickier if Democrats flip control of the House, because Jeffries’s ascension to the Speakership will hinge on his ability to win 218 votes on the floor in the first week of January. That task will require the support of all Democrats, from battleground centrists who are cold to aggressive impeachments, to incoming democratic socialists who might view the vote on Hegseth’s removal as a gauge of Jeffries’s leadership credentials.

Jeffries has taken pains to balance those pressures by attacking Hegseth’s track record and calling for his firing while refusing to say if he’ll support impeachment.

“We haven’t ruled anything out when it comes to all of the tools available to us to hold people accountable, and we haven’t ruled anything in. That’s been our position. That will remain our position,” Jeffries told reporters in the Capitol last week.

“Pete Hegseth should’ve never been confirmed. This guy is the most unqualified so-called secretary of war in American history,” he added. “He’s the architect of Operation Epic Failure in Iran that has increased gas prices on everyday Americans and further burdened them economically. … It’s my view that’s the reason why [GOP leaders] pulled the resolution, because there were Republicans who can’t even defend Pete Hegseth at this point.”

The resolution in question, sponsored by Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.), features eight articles of impeachment accusing Hegseth of abuses of power related to his handling of the Iran war, a failure to protect civilians and the extrajudicial killings of alleged drug smugglers in international waters, among other charges. Massie introduced the proposal as a privileged resolution, which forces a floor vote even over the objections of GOP leaders.

Johnson evaded that vote by cutting the House calendar a day short last week. But the clock resumes when the House returns on Nov. 9, making Hegseth’s impeachment a first order of business in the lame-duck session.

Democrats have seized on Johnson’s decision, saying Republicans simply feared taking a tough vote ahead of the midterms — an attack that’s allowed them to highlight the unpopular Iran war.

“You talk to Republicans here — which I do a lot, because I’m on the Armed Services and Intel committee — a vast majority of people do not like Pete Hegseth. They think he’s incompetent, at best. They think he’s a clown and a joker at worst. … And a lot of people are somewhere in between,” said Rep. Jason Crow (D-Colo.). “They don’t want to vote on it.”

Johnson has rejected that narrative as “ridiculous,” saying he simply wanted to grant lawmakers more time to campaign.

But attacking Johnson over the process is different from throwing your weight behind impeachment. Even after the vote was delayed, Democratic leaders distanced themselves from Massie’s resolution and promoted a more deliberative process.

“The DOD mismanagement is incredibly clear, but let’s be honest. The only calls, the only discussions about impeachment in the halls of Congress this week have been from Republicans to impeach Pete Hegseth. No Democratic members were making those calls,” said Rep. Pete Aguilar (Calif.), the chair of the House Democratic Caucus.

“We believe in oversight and accountability — that is a hallmark of what this chamber should be doing,” he continued. “We will do that job. We will do it in a thoughtful way.”

Aguilar’s remarks ignored another impeachment push just before the recess, when Democratic Rep. Al Green (Texas) forced a vote to remove Trump over the killing of several civilians by immigration enforcement officers. Many Democrats were furious with Green for distracting from the party’s economic message, and every member of leadership sought to balance competing internal interests by voting “present” — a strategy that could forecast how they’ll approach the Hegseth resolution.

However, heading into that vote, at least one powerful Democrat said Massie has made “very compelling” points about the laws of war and the possibility that Hegseth violated them, which could make it tough for Democrats to do anything but support impeachment.

“He raises a bunch of profound arguments,” Raskin said, “and I’m taking it extremely seriously.”

articles.title: Karoline Leavitt says some White House reporters privately apologized for asking 'unfair' questions
articles.summary: Karoline Leavitt says White House reporters privately apologized for asking questions their bosses demanded, calling them "unfair" during briefings.
articles.body: Former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said that some reporters covering the White House privately apologized to her for asking questions they acknowledged were "unfair." Leavitt made the comments on the latest episode of "Hang Out with Sean Hannity" while discussing the "performative" nature of press briefings. "There's been times reporters have even said to me, ‘I'm sorry I had to ask that today. My bosses really wanted me to ask that, they know it's an unfair question,’" she said, without naming names. TRUMP ANNOUNCES WHITE HOUSE BAN AGAINST THREE MEDIA OUTLETS Leavitt, who frequently sparred with reporters during her tenure as press secretary, argued that journalists at major news organizations are often beholden to the demands of their superiors. "The reporters are controlled by their bosses… They're not in control of their own livelihood," she told host Sean Hannity. "They are dictated by the editors and the execs at some of these companies." DAVID MARCUS: KAROLINE LEAVITT’S LASTING LEGACY IS OPENING THE WHITE HOUSE TO INDIE PRESS Leavitt said both the media and administration officials behind the podium contribute to political theatrics in the briefing room. "There's a performative aspect to the briefing room," she conceded. "In fairness, I think on both sides, right? But definitely with the press. And they have to do that because their bosses are demanding it." Despite frequently clashing with reporters, including CNN’s Kaitlan Collins, and sometimes referring to other members of the press as "left-wing hacks," Leavitt said she has no ill will toward journalists. "I don't hate anyone," she insisted. "There are some I enjoy less than others. I'll say that… There's some that I just don't take seriously because they are just left-wing hacks, as I would call them in the briefing room." SCOTT PELLEY SAYS CBS NEWS IS ‘ON FIRE’ AFTER BARI WEISS TAKEOVER AND ‘60 MINUTES’ BLOODBATH Leavitt credited "a few" solid reporters but refrained from naming them, concerned that if she did, she would "kill their career." She also said she has observed what she considers positive shifts in leadership at some major news organizations, pointing to "a lot of improvement" at CBS, while still claiming bias elsewhere. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "We're seeing some changes at some networks, but most of them are controlled by far-left liberals who live in New York or D.C., and they dictate what's asked and what's written," Leavitt argued. "We are not asking for like positive puff pieces every day, just fairness, truth, accuracy, just telling a story or writing about factual information," she added. Leavitt’s full interview on the latest episode "Hang Out with Sean Hannity" is available on YouTube, Spotify and Apple.

articles.title: Republican candidates highlight healthcare in 2026, battling voter distrust
articles.summary: Health care is shaping up to be a vulnerability for the GOP in the 2026 midterm elections, when Democrats hope to capture the House and Senate.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — Facing a challenging re-election bid, seven-term Rep. Scott Perry, R-Pa., says he’s not surprised that voters distrust the Republican Party to improve their healthcare. “I can’t say that Republicans have done much about it,” Perry told NBC News before the House left last week for a lengthy election recess. “We’ve even passed some things here, but they don’t make it anywhere in the Senate. So, you know, people want results, not talk.” Healthcare is shaping up to be a vulnerability for the GOP in the 2026 midterm elections, when Democrats hope to capture the House and the Senate. According to this month’s NBC News poll, voters trust Democrats over Republicans on healthcare by 22 points. A New York Times-Siena College poll similarly found that likely voters preferred Democrats by 24 points on the issue. Still, Republicans are leaning in and highlighting the issue, with many of them using populist rhetoric criticizing insurance and drug companies. The goal, according to three GOP strategists, is more about trying to narrow the Democratic advantage than expecting to win on the issue. In ultracompetitive Michigan, Senate candidate Mike Rogers is running an ad inveighing against high prescription drug costs relative to Canada. Rogers, a former Republican congressman who is calling for price transparency rules for hospitals and insurers, held an event Saturday attacking Democratic rival Abdul El-Sayed’s “Medicare for All” proposal. “I just can’t think of a more important issue to the people of Michigan than healthcare — their costs, their rising costs and how we get to the bottom of it,” Rogers said at the healthcare-focused event in Taylor. “He wants Medicare for all. I want Medicare for seniors. They’ve earned it, they’ve worked for it, let’s improve it, let’s get it going.” In Iowa, Republican Senate candidate Ashley Hinson launched an ad in May saying “healthcare companies are ripping you off” and that she’s “working with President Trump to take on big insurance companies.” In a New Jersey swing district, Republican Rep. Tom Kean is running an ad lamenting that too many families “suffer because of big insurance companies.” Kean, who missed four months of work in the House citing treatment for depression, touted his bill to boost Labor Department authority to enforce mental health rules for insurance plans. Even in deep red Kansas, Republican Sen. Roger Marshall is running an ad that credits him for “standing up to big insurance.” Democrats are blasting the $1 trillion in Medicaid spending cuts that Republicans passed on party lines in President Donald Trump’s “big, beautiful bill,” as well as a pot of Obamacare funding that Republicans successfully pushed to end last year. Those two moves are estimated to cause more than 10 million people in the U.S. to lose coverage or, for those on Affordable Care Act, pay more for insurance. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., has vowed to restore the Medicaid and ACA funds as Democrats’ top priority if they capture House control. “When you scratch the surface, healthcare is always an important issue to voters. And it’s an issue to try to talk to swing women voters and other subgroups of swing voters,” said Republican pollster Bill McInturff, who co-conducts the NBC News poll with Democratic pollster Jeff Horwitt. “Republicans need to make up a deficit with women voters, and when you ask women what they are most focused on, healthcare always scores very high,” McInturff said, while adding: “You don’t have to win an issue. You just have to compete on the issue.” According to NBC News polling, Democrats have consistently led on healthcare since the early 1990s. Their edge topped 30 points in 2008, ahead of a blue wave, and it fell to as little as 7 points in 2010, a red wave year. And while Republicans spent much of the last decade, including Trump’s first term, attempting to repeal or undo the ACA, the party has never coalesced around an alternative. The party has long favored curtailing healthcare funding to align with its support for tax cuts, a position that is coming into conflict with its growing reliance on working-class voters. Hinson, Kean and Marshall all voted for the Medicaid cuts. All but Kean voted against resurrecting ACA money. Rogers, who left Congress in 2015, has not said whether he’d support reviving the ACA funds, and his campaign had no comment about how he’d vote on reversing Medicaid cuts in Trump’s megabill last year. “Michiganders see through Mike Rogers’ B.S. and understand that if he’s elected to the Senate, Rogers will eagerly continue his life’s work as Big Pharma’s greatest champion,” said Cole Wozniak, a spokesperson for El-Sayed, who has also vowed to restore the Medicaid and ACA money. “Michiganders deserve far better, which is why Dr. Abdul El-Sayed is running to fight back against Big Pharma and deliver Medicare for All.” The White House’s internal polling shows that the administration’s work to lower drug prices is one of its most popular second term achievements, and it has encouraged Republican candidates to run on those issues, according to a senior White House official. But when Trump held an event Friday to tout his most favored nation pricing policies for certain drugs under Medicaid, his message was drowned out by his just-announced decision to ban some news outlets from the White House. Republicans who write healthcare legislation have also not made clear what they would do about healthcare if they maintain control of Congress. Sen. Mike Crapo, R-Idaho, the chair of the Finance Committee that oversees healthcare policy, told NBC News his agenda next year will include “PBM fixes” — referring to third-party pharmacy benefit managers — and tackling “inefficiencies.” Beyond that, he didn’t provide specifics. “Our healthcare system is broken. I’m not going to tell you what the solutions are yet,” Crapo said. “So, I guess my response would be that we’re going to need to continue diving into the various issues from A to Z, and try to address the shortfalls and fix them. I think we’ve got a lot of good minds working on it.”

articles.title: China’s Xi set to arrive in Washington for high-stakes Trump summit as AI supremacy battle looms large
articles.summary: China's President Xi Jinping arrives for a tense White House summit with Trump covering AI, tariffs, rare earth minerals and fentanyl exports.
articles.body: China's President Xi Jinping is set to arrive on U.S. soil later Wednesday for what is expected to be a tense showdown between President Donald Trump and the communist leader. A red carpet rollout is planned for when Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, arrive at Joint Base Andrews on Wednesday evening, replete with an arrival ceremony for the man who has found himself at odds with Trump on issues ranging from artificial intelligence and intellectual property theft, trade practices, rare-earth minerals to the communist country's support for Iran during America's military conflict there. Xi hasn't visited the nation's capital in more than a decade. AI will be a major topic of discussion during the two-day summit, which officially begins Thursday morning and ends Friday evening, according to a senior administration official. Thursday will begin with a prestigious State Arrival Ceremony, including 479 military personnel from all branches on the South Lawn, State Floor and Rose Garden of the White House. XI PREPARES CHINA ‘FOR BATTLE’ AS EXPERT WARNS OF GRAVE DANGER FACING US AHEAD OF DC SUMMIT According to the official, a wide-ranging deal on possible tariff reductions on non-strategic goods is an expected topic of discussion, who also said the nation's leaders will discuss rare-earth exports and possible export controls. Trump is also expected to press China to do more to curb fentanyl precursor chemical exports. Trump is also likely to press for the release of an American who has been wrongfully detained in China, Gulshan Abbas, who has languished in a Chinese prison for eight years. The country accused her of "participating in a terrorist organization" after her sister spoke out about China's genocide of Uyghurs, according to Forbes. House Speaker Mike Johnson and other Republicans have expressed confidence that Trump will push for her release. articles.title: Ex-Democrat shares abortion pill experience that left her 'hemorrhaging in the bath'
articles.summary: Haile McAnally says she nearly bled to death after taking abortion pills and is now heading to Capitol Hill to curb mail-order mifepristone.
articles.body: Nebraska resident Haile McAnally believes it was "divine intervention" that saved her from bleeding to death in her own bathroom shortly after high school. She told Fox News Digital that abortion medication, in the form of pills, was to blame for her having "hemorrhaged in the bath," and that she is now focused on sparing other women the same possible fate. "Planned Parenthood told us that this is what is women empowerment. This is what women do when they can't handle it. They take this route, and they don't acknowledge the pain it causes," McAnally said. "The same pills I took under direction of medical professionals, they can be shipped anywhere at any time," she continued. "I can't imagine being a young woman in college and maybe finding herself in this position, ordering these pills online, not knowing what kind of maybe pre-medical condition she has, and she finds herself in the same position." FIRST ON FOX: TOP REPUBLICANS TAKE ABORTION PILL FIGHT TO SUPREME COURT, CITING COERCION AND SAFETY RISKS McAnally said the experience is also part of what motivated her to switch parties from a pro-choice "registered Democrat" to a pro-life Republican. "I had always been on the left because I thought they were the side that was more open to having these conversations, the free-thinkers," she recalled. McAnally said her questions about how and why her ordeal happened were met with, "You can't talk about it. You can't talk about it because it's not part of our agenda. It's not a part of our platform to talk about any complications this may have." "I noticed the more I asked questions, the people on the right were more willing to talk about it, which, in the pro-life space, I thought I was gonna be condemned. I thought it was gonna like, 'You're gonna go to hell. This is horrible. You're a murderer.' These things that you always hear from the left that the right is gonna call you," she said. And I was like, 'I'm gonna talk about it and see what happens.' And the right was so forgiving and so loving and really embraced my story and really said, 'This is horrible, I'm glad you seek forgiveness and counsel for this.'" McAnally told Fox News Digital that it had always been her dream to become a mother. When she got pregnant by her boyfriend, however, she said he had a very different response. "He asked me what I was gonna do about it and hung up the phone, and I haven't talked to him since," she said. She recalled being fearful of going through the experience alone and turning to pro-choice groups for guidance. "I remember seeing the pink signs everywhere and the marketing that says ... the sisterhood will take care of you," she said. "And as someone in that position where you're scared, and you are looking for answers somewhere, and you don't wanna be alone and being so young at the time, that was a very enticing message." PLANNED PARENTHOOD ACROSS MIDWEST AT RISK DUE TO LACK OF FEDERAL FUNDS AFTER 3 FACILITIES CLOSE IN MICHIGAN McAnally described the clinic as being "cold," "dark," and smelling of rubbing alcohol. "They took my money, and they sent me back to this room where ... this doctor was going to walk me through everything that was going to happen that day. That's the consent kind of happened, in that room, and he didn't know me from Adam. He really didn't ask about my background and anything medical that's ever happened," she recalled. ABORTION PILL FIGHT HEADS TO SUPREME COURT AS MANUFACTURER WARNS OF ‘CHAOS’ AFTER RULING But as an "emotional and scared" young woman, McAnally said she signed the consent forms and was given one abortion pill and told to take a second one at home. She said medical staff warned her it would feel like "a more intense period," recommending a heating pad and tea for comfort. "I followed that protocol, went home, took the second pill, and I found myself on the toilet in the bathroom where bleeding occurred, which was exactly what they said. But after about two hours, I was still bleeding out. And I started feeling really weak. I knew that what was happening was not right, but I couldn't really comprehend what was going on," McAnally said. I CHOSE ABORTION, THEN CHANGED MY MIND — CALIFORNIA WANTS THAT CHOICE GONE She said she dragged herself into the bathtub before realizing her condition had quickly become serious — but that her phone was out of reach. "I just laid there and thought that was the moment that everything was over, and, partially, I felt like it was punishment for me making that decision," she said. "But at the end of the day, I remember waking up, and I was in the hospital and my friend had come home, and she had realized that I was laying in the bathtub unconscious at the time, and she called 911, and I had a blood transfusion done." McAnally said she now feels like it's her duty to warn other women of the potential dangers of unfettered access to mifepristone. That's why she and several other women allied with anti-abortion group Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America are heading to Capitol Hill on Thursday to meet with lawmakers and staffers. Their plea: curb access to mail-order abortion pills. "Women who’ve suffered the devastating effects of abortion drugs who are clear-eyed about the lies of the Big Abortion industry are the most effective advocates," said SBA Pro-Life America President Marjorie Dannenfelser. "Their lives are forever changed, but they’re standing strong and having a powerful impact on Capitol Hill and beyond." A study in JAMA Internal Medicine observed that 0.6% of women who get mail-order abortion pills experience medical emergencies that leave them hospitalized. A conflicting study by the Ethics and Public Policy Center said one in 10 women have a "serious adverse event."
