articles.title: 25 years after 9/11, terrorism has entered the AI era — we must adapt
articles.summary: In addition to boosting their outreach, recruitment, and fundraising, helps terrorists identify vulnerabilities and targets. It will help them plan attacks faster and with fewer human resources.
articles.body:
Twenty-five years after 9/11, we are entering a new era of terrorism. In recent weeks, authorities have arrested individuals who pledged allegiance to ISIS and used artificial intelligence to help plan major attacks.

Although those plots were thwarted, they reveal that terrorist organizations are now using AI in far more consequential ways. AI can help “novices” to build chemical and biological weapons . This rapidly evolving threat requires an immediate plan of action.

The July 2004 9/11 Commission Report underlined the need for foresight, information sharing, and adaptability to prevent additional major terrorist attacks. It warned the most important failure by our nation and its security agencies to foresee the threat “was one of imagination,” something needed today for addressing terrorist groups embrace of AI.

Since 9/11, jihadis have had at their disposal a succession of new technologies, but AI is the most significant. Technical skills that once demanded specialized expertise are disappearing and obstacles once faced, already eroded by technological developments, are now almost completely removed.

Today, every major terrorist group sees AI as a game changer and have all used it for a range of purposes: propaganda and media production, recruitment and outreach, cyber operations, digital warfare (including drones and weapons), operational guidance, training in data science and digital media, and integrating advanced technologies.

While Al-Qaeda incorporates AI into its long-term plans, ISIS – whose base is younger and more tech-savvy – uses it for immediate media and operational impact, including recruitment and coordinating “lone wolf” attacks.

AI has been described as a “capability multiplier” for jihadis. It began in March 2025 with AI-generated videos of ISIS operatives reading news reports and continued with this year’s AI-generated English translations from ISIS newsletters. As one ISIS supporter put it , “In order to move forward in the future, we need to learn how to use the new technology.”

These first forays were eclipsed by the exposure of jihadis’ fixation on AI chatbots. On August 21, Canadian authorities arrested a Montreal teen suspected of planning a terror attack at a school using AI. On Aug. 18, a Somali-born Briton was convicted of preparing acts of terrorism; he had traveled to Syria in an attempt to become a “martyr” for ISIS after interacting with an AI chatbot used by ISIS recruiters.

Cambridge terrorism researcher Antonia Juelich reported this summer that Boko Haram in Nigeria is turning to AI chatbots for tactical on-the-ground advantages, including directly on the battlefield. Exactly six years earlier, in August 2020, I published an extensive report on jihadi use of bots — precursors to today’s AI assistants in terms of user interaction — on the encrypted messaging platform Telegram: for planning attacks, sharing information on training, making weapons and bombs, disseminating news, and recruiting.

The period since represents a largely wasted time for preparing for today when AI became a weapon in the hands of terrorists. On Aug. 31, as part of a review of the 9/11 Commission Report, the House Intelligence Committee released a report raising concerns about the threat of terrorism posed by the advancement of AI and called for “preventing terrorist groups from developing access to equipment and expertise.”

However, the greatest concern of jihadis using AI should be chatter on closed and encrypted apps. Take for example, in January 2026 a discussion on explosives and drones by ISIS supporters who mulled attacking Trump Tower in New York City, using AI for operational guidance.

Just like everyone these days, jihadi groups are also having internal debates about the normalization of AI. A featured article in an issue of the Islamic State Khurasan Province “Voice of Khurasan” provided guidelines for its “ethical” and safe use, while a user on an encrypted Al-Qaeda platform recently accused readers of sharing AI-generated posts, speculating that their accounts had been taken over by intelligence agents.

Why is terrorist adoption of AI significant? In addition to boosting their outreach, recruitment, and fundraising, it will help them identify vulnerabilities and targets and plan attacks faster and with fewer human resources.

Also, while a major concern today is the technological race to prevent Chinese AI supremacy, we should think of all worst-case possibilities – image a jihadi AI startup made up of programmers who develop their own software to share with those seeking to perpetrate terror attacks. They have openly recruited for AI expertise.

Thwarting this will not be easy. It will require a network of researchers constantly monitoring what they are saying openly and in private and studying where they have succeeded and failed so far. It will take cooperation, responsibility, and commitment on the part of AI companies. And it will demand the foresight, information sharing, and adaptability outlined in the 9/11 Commission Report to prevent a recurrence of the failure of imagination that allowed that attack to happen.

Steven Stalinsky Ph.D. is Executive Director of MEMRI .

articles.title: Fight over Trump’s media ban heads to court
articles.summary: In today’s issue: ▪ Media outlets’ day in court ▪ Trump at the U.N. ▪ GOP senator calls for Don Jr. probe ▪ Susan Collins under scrutiny The battle over President Trump’s ban of three media outlets from the White House is turning to the legal system starting today with a hearing on whether the move…
articles.body:
The battle over President Trump ’s ban of three media outlets from the White House is turning to the legal system starting today with a hearing on whether the move is constitutional.

Trump has already said he expects to lose when the case goes before U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly , whom Trump appointed during his first term. He reiterated Tuesday that he is bracing for a loss “because this is a judge who is not a particularly fair judge,” but declined to say whether he would comply with the judge’s order.

“I think we have a right to clean out fake news,” he told reporters during one of many meetings at the UN General Assembly.

Kelly was the judge who presided over the case in 2018 in which Trump revoked White House press credentials from Jim Acosta , then a CNN correspondent. Kelly ruled in favor of Acosta, directing that his credentials be returned while the legal battle played out. The White House eventually reversed its decision and restored Acosta’s pass.

Ahead of the hearing, the Department of Justice (DOJ) argued in a court filing late Tuesday that the ban shouldn’t be blocked. The filing cites national security concerns and alleges that the outlets “failed to meet basic minimum ‘standards or professionalism and decorum.’”

“After all, access to the White House is a privilege—not a right,” the filing argues.

If Kelly were to rule in favor of the news outlets, an appeal would be almost certain to quickly follow. A favorable ruling could mean outlets quickly regain access to the White House, effectively ending a standoff that has left with White House without a television press pool.

The major television networks that rotate covering the president are all continuing to sit out the pool, which takes turns recording Trump’s every public move, in solidarity with the three banned outlets. The impacts of their decision were on display Monday when Trump was inaudible while speaking at a ribbon-cutting ceremony unveiling the new helipad on the South Lawn of the White House.

“This is one example of it backfiring just a little bit,” a Newsmax anchor remarked.

The White House launched a 24/7 stream on YouTube called Trump TV following the ban.

At today’s hearing, the outlets are expected to argue the ban violates their First Amendment rights. The Hill’s Dominick Mastrangelo reports most media and legal observers expect the organizations to succeed and their journalists to soon be back on White House grounds.

Still, the battle marks the biggest confrontation yet in years of brawls between the Trump administration and the media.

Trump didn’t cite national security when he first announced the bans, saying he made the decision because of the “constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS.” He also has signaled other outlets or journalists could soon be banned too.

The administration faced off with The Associated Press last year after the wire service refused to refer to the Gulf of Mexico as the “Gulf of America,” in line with an executive order the president issued. The White House limited AP journalists’ access to Air Force One and the Oval Office and kicked the outlet out of the press pool in response.

A federal judge initially sided with AP, but an appeals court largely overturned the ruling. The case is still ongoing, but the AP has regained normal access in the meantime.

The hearing Wednesday is scheduled for 3:30 p.m., and a ruling could come at that point or soon afterward.

You can read more this morning about what to expect in the case from The Hill newsletter The Gavel , which covers the biggest stories in the legal world each week. Click here to sign up to get the newsletter in your inbox.

TRUMP’S BIG DECISION : Trump threatened to “annihilate” Iran, in remarks before the United Nations General Assembly yesterday, but he still left open the possibility of striking a deal with the country.

“I have a big decision to make,” Trump said in his speech. “Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before, maybe one of the greatest in the Middle East or even the world? Or do I annihilate the Islamic republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?”

The president later said U.S. officials had a three-hour meeting with Iranians on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly, describing it as a “very productive meeting” with another scheduled in the “very near future.”

“They had a very good meeting, and we’ll see how it turns out,” Trump said. “But, certainly, it’s to their advantage to make a deal.”

Also on the sidelines of the summit, Trump signed a trilateral security agreement with Greenland and Denmark that gives the U.S. permanent military rights in Greenland. Trump announced during his speech that the U.S. will “immediately begin” development of two “very major military bases” on the Arctic island.

Trump also held a series of bilateral meetings on the sidelines of the forum, including with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and Venezuelan leader Delcy Rodríguez .

Trump said he supports a ban on diesel exports, when asked during his bilat with Zelensky whether such a proposal was under consideration, saying, “I’ve called for it within my people. I’ve been talking about it.”

“We’re examining that, whether it’s feasible in terms of the overall refining capacity and whether a full or partial ban would work,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent added, when prompted by Trump to expound on the issue.

The U.S. president also held his first in-person meeting with U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham , whom Trump praised as a “natural businessperson.”

TRUMP JR. ON THE SPOT: Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah) is asking Senate Judiciary Committee leaders to subpoena Donald Trump Jr. and Hunter Biden and launch investigations into the “use of presidential family relationships” for financial benefit, preferential treatment or access by domestic or foreign interests.

“The country should not have to accept one standard for the family of a Republican president and another for the family of a Democratic president. Nor should congressional oversight begin and end when control of the White House changes hands,” Curtis wrote in his letter to Sens. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) and Dick Durbin (D-Ill.), the committee’s chair and ranking member, respectively.

Curtis said reports about foreign interests using the presidents’ sons to gain access to their powerful fathers “raise legitimate questions about foreign access to members of a sitting president’s family and whether such a relationship can create actual or perceived expectations of favorable treatment.”

The call from a GOP senator for the committee to subpoena the son of a sitting president of his own party is striking, particularly just weeks away from the midterm elections. Two other key GOP senators on the Judiciary Committee, John Cornyn and Thom Tillis , said Tuesday that they support Curtis’s push .

Grassley, not so much. He told The Hill Tuesday that he hadn’t read Curtis’s letter and said there are other demands for the committee’s time.

ACA CUTS: The Trump administration announced that nearly 760,000 people will be removed from Affordable Care Act (ACA) coverage, citing alleged fraudulent enrollment.

“These are not real people. We’re not paying insurance for nonexistent ghosts,” Dr. Mehmet Oz , administrator for the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS), said at a White House press conference.

Officials said the cancellations would save an estimated $2.2 billion in taxpayer funds. Oz also said approximately 35 percent of people currently on ObamaCare exchanges have never used their insurance.

The effort, which was spearheaded by Vice President Vance ’s White House Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, is “not about cutting off anybody from their benefits,” Vance said. “ It’s about cutting off fraudsters from stealing from these programs.”

However, health care policy experts and former officials are warning that the process lacked transparency and likely removed a significant number of legitimate subscribers.

“I would imagine we’ll hear from some subset of consumers that ask: why did my enrollment get cancelled?” Ellen Montz, a former deputy CMS administrator under Biden, told NPR .

FULL KISSINGER : The president has declared Secretary of State Marco Rubio to be the permanent national security adviser , ending his acting stint in the role that’s lasted for more than a year.

Rubio was named acting national security adviser in May after Mike Waltz stepped down from his role in the aftermath of the “Signalgate” controversy in which a journalist was included in a private group chat on the messaging app Signal with high-ranking officials discussing a military operation against the Houthis in Yemen.

Waltz later was nominated and confirmed as U.N. ambassador.

Rubio became the first person to hold both roles since Henry Kissinger , who served during the Nixon and Ford administrations.

Rubio has worn several hats during Trump’s second term and earned praise from the president for his ability to juggle multiple responsibilities. It’s also at times been a source of humor at the many jobs Rubio has held, which included acting archivist of the U.S. and acting head of the U.S. Agency for International Development.

FIELD TEST : Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Tuesday that the Pentagon is altering its promotion process for reaching the rank of general to “cut bureaucracy and demand true meritocracy” for senior ranks.

Hegseth said the department will roll out the Joint Warfighter Evaluation, a battlefield-style assessment for eligible colonels and Navy captains. The program will screen officers on their “ability to fight, adapt and win.”

Internal documents obtained by The Hill show each branch of the military will have their own version of the evaluation.

Hegseth said commanders should be chosen by “proven competence, not paper credential.” He has repeatedly broken with precedent throughout his time atop the Pentagon, blocking many promotions to one-star general or admiral, many of them Black and female service members.

Preschool teacher Melissa Mowbray works with AI on her laptop at Academic Magnet High School during the Charleston County School District Charleston Educator Symposium on July 22, 2026 in North Charleston, S.C. (Mic Smith, Associated Press)

AI CONUNDRUM: Schools are struggling to find the best path forward on regulating artificial intelligence use in the classroom, as they balance concerns about its potential negative effects on learning against the risk of leaving students underprepared for an ever-evolving workforce, The Hill’s Lexi Lonas Cochran reports .

The two largest school districts in the country — the Los Angeles Unified School District and New York City Public Schools — have now put a one-year moratorium on generative AI usage in the classroom.

In New York City, Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) said the one-year pause applies only to public schools through eighth grade. Select high school classrooms will be allowed to use AI pilot platforms, and high schoolers will take two AI critical thinking classes during this academic year.

“The tech industry wants us to believe that AI in early education is not only inevitable, but that it is necessary,” Mamdani said. “We do not see it that way.”

But there is also a growing recognition of the importance of AI in the workforce, which has led to school districts taking different approaches for students of different ages.

Tameka Royal , the CEO of Democracy Prep Public Schools, a system of charter schools in New York City, said the one-year moratorium is intended to give time for schools to study evidence, train educators and establish guardrails and policies that don’t yet exist around AI.

“This is not a pause that turns into avoidance,” Royal said, adding, “You’re determining where does AI expand access without replacing students’ thinking.”

“The push here is, for our high school students, the lessons to be about what are the tools and how do I use them responsibly and to really help elevate and enhance the work that I’m doing,” she added. “And then for our youngest students, it’s the taking a pause to truly understand what it means for them.”

UNDER THE MISCROSCOPE : Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) is under heightened scrutiny with her key Senate race coming into the homestretch, following a report that she was a subject of an FBI corruption investigation.

ProPublica reported Tuesday that the head of Collins’s super PAC, Scott Reed , during her 2020 Senate reelection campaign worked with Martin Kao , the head of a defense contractor called Navatek, to direct donations to the senator’s campaign in exchange for government contracts in Maine.

The outlet reported that Kao sent an initial $150,000 donation to Collins’s super PAC through a shell company, hiding that a government contractor — which is banned from making political contributions — sent the money.

Seven days after the super PAC cashed the check, ProPublica reported, one of its employees emailed a Navatek lobbyist asking for Kao’s phone number: “Senator Collins would like to call Martin to thank him.”

Kao reportedly told Navatek executives two months later that Collins committed to getting the company $32 million in naval contracts.

The report states that the investigation was heating up in 2024 and the FBI was prepared to investigate further the following year. The agents had enough evidence for a sweeping bribery probe that could have drawn in members of both parties.

But once Trump came in in 2025, the teams handling public corruption cases at the FBI and DOJ were gutted, killing the investigation.

Annie Clark , Collins’s deputy chief of staff, called the allegations “categorically false” and accused ProPublica of taking the word of an untrustworthy source in Kao. The now-former CEO pleaded guilty to multiple charges, including money laundering and wire fraud, and made the claims to investigators as he was seeking to receive a more lenient sentence.

ProPublica pushed back on Clark’s assertion, saying the outlet has the receipts to back up the claims, much of which it independently corroborated with a “trove of evidence.”

Democratic Senate nominee Troy Jackson ’s campaign was quick to denounce Collins over the report, calling it “corruption of the highest order.”

“We deserve answers about every contract and every conversation that Collins and her team facilitated on the backs of taxpayers. The jig is up,” Jackson said in a statement.

The single reached its 23rd week atop the charts this week, surpassing Mariah Carey ’s “All I Want for Christmas is You.” The song has been rising in the rankings of longest-running top singles in recent weeks, seeing Langley first become the longest-running artist with a non-holiday song when she surpassed “Old Town Road” by Lil Nas X and Billy Ray Cyrus and Shaboozey ’s “A Bar Song” last month.

The industry and analytics company Luminate found “Choosin’ Texas” brought in more than 900 million on-demand streams in the U.S. and more than 1.25 billion globally as of mid-last month, according to The Associated Press .

Questions remain as to how much longer Langley’s single will stay at No.1 and whether Carey’s hit holiday song can retake the top spot later this year. “All I Want for Christmas is You” has returned to the top spot each December over the past several years.

articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: House Democrats paved the way for President Donald Trump's anti-fraud division to survive beyond his presidency, but one Republican fears it'll be a different outcome in the Senate. Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., shared with Fox News Digital that he was introducing legislation that would make the National Fraud Enforcement Division permanent. It comes after a bill to do the same thing cruised through the House. The lawmaker made it official Tuesday night when the Senate reopened for business. But the Senate is a different political animal, and Democrats’ possible reticence to give Trump a win before the midterm elections may thwart his plan. Schmitt, during an interview with Fox News Digital, contended that since the sprawling Minnesota fraud scandal was unveiled earlier this year, Democrats have been on the back foot. DEMOCRATS RELUCTANTLY HAND TRUMP MAJOR VICTORY ON FRAUD PROGRAM TARGETING TIM WALZ "They're very defensive about it, and you know the fact is that you had — maybe it had something to do with this sort of toxic empathy or suicidal empathy [they] have done on immigration where you had these Somali fraudsters and maybe, maybe their instinct to defend every group of people that came here from somewhere else, even if they're defrauding the American people, overrode their logic." Still, House Democrats, including House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., begrudgingly gave Trump a win last week and voted to make his anti-fraud task force permanent. That bipartisan vote comes as Democrats are reconciling with their messaging on rooting out waste, fraud and abuse. And New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who has increasingly been one of the progressive leaders of the party, warned Democrats had ceded ground on issues like quality of life and rooting out waste and fraud, and that finding waste had taken hold as a "right-wing concern" rather than an issue Democrats could champion. DEMOCRATS BEGRUDGINGLY HAND TRUMP VICTORY ON TARIFFS IN SPRAWLING SANCTIONS BILL "I know that we live in a hyper-partisan age, I get that," Schmitt said. "But there are some things I don't think should be partisan. Saving taxpayer money should be something we're all focused on." "I mean these are criminals who, you know, are stealing from American taxpayers and the potential beneficiaries of important programs," he continued. Trump first announced the creation of a new division within the Department of Justice (DOJ) to combat fraud in January 2026 following reports of staggering fraud taking place in the backyard of one of his political enemies: Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz. TRUMP SAYS ANTI-FRAUD EFFORTS ARE UNCOVERING BILLIONS IN WASTE, CLAIMS SAVINGS COULD BALANCE BUDGET The unit embedded in the DOJ was officially launched under then-acting Attorney General Todd Blanche, with the goal of targeting "fraud affecting the federal government, federally funded programs, and private citizens," according to a release by the administration. It’s chaired by Vice President JD Vance, who Trump tapped to be his de facto fraud czar, and run by Assistant Attorney General Colin McDonald. Schmitt argued that "having permanence in the Department of Justice will be important so that, no matter who is president, that this remains a focus." "To me, this shouldn't be a partisan issue at all," Schmitt said. "But sadly, we live in a world where Democrats aren't as focused on this, but I think we've got an administration that is." And Schmitt leads the Senate’s Anti-Fraud Taskforce, launched in June, that includes only Republican members. That wasn’t by design. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP He said that they had extended an invitation to "Republicans and Democrats alike," but only one side of the aisle accepted the call. "I was a little surprised. I think some offices took a look at it and, for whatever reason, didn't want to be part of the effort," Schmitt said. "I don't understand that." "But, you know, of course, the offer remains open if anybody wants to," he continued. "I just think that this is something that our people back home expect us to work together on. And I don't understand why you wouldn't want to be a part of an anti-fraud task force."

articles.title: Supreme Court declines to intervene in case of surrogate mother who refused abortion
articles.summary: McKenna West's surrogacy custody fight over a baby with hypoplastic left heart syndrome hit the Supreme Court after she fled to Texas to avoid an abortion.
articles.body: The U.S. Supreme Court declined Tuesday to intervene in the case of a surrogate mother who refused to have an abortion and is now seeking custody of the child. McKenna West gave birth to the boy, whom she named Gabriel, in Texas in August after she fled from California when the parents asked her to abort the child over a heart defect. She argued in Texas court that she should maintain custody over the child despite the surrogacy agreement, but a judge in Texas ruled against her. West then appealed to the Supreme Court, but Justice Elena Kagan, who handles cases arising from California, declined to hear the case on Tuesday without issuing a written decision. SURROGATE GIVES BIRTH IN TEXAS TO BABY WITH HEART DEFECT AFTER PARENTS REQUESTED ABORTION The intended parents, Omar Ahmed and Nausheen Gilkar, signed a surrogacy agreement with West in August 2025. They point to a clause in the agreement that allowed for a termination of pregnancy in the case of a "fetal abnormality." The child, whom they had named Rumi, was diagnosed with hypoplastic left heart syndrome, which causes part of the heart to be underdeveloped and prevents normal blood flow. The child underwent surgery in Texas and is now "suffering from potential complications" related to the operation. HHS WARNS TEXAS HOSPITALS AGAINST DENYING LIFE-SAVING CARE TO NEWBORN WITH DISABILITY Ahmed and Gilkar attempted to force West to have an abortion when the defect was initially detected, but West refused and fled to Texas, where she received support from Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton. Paxton signed an order stating that the child must receive lifesaving care in Texas. The case went up to the Texas Supreme Court, which ruled last week that the child could be moved to California, where the intended parents have lined up plans for medical care. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Ahmed and Gilkar first sought out a surrogacy agreement after attempts at in vitro fertilization failed. The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: Socialist mayor’s new answer to rampant retail crime ignites fury: ‘Bandage on a bullet wound’
articles.summary: Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson's $1.7 million grocery store security plan draws fierce criticism from those demanding the city arrest and prosecute criminals.
articles.body: Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson is rolling out city-funded security for grocery stores facing theft, break-ins and vandalism, fueling criticism that Seattle is spending taxpayer money to protect businesses from crime instead of doing enough to stop it in the first place. The socialist mayor announced the rollout of the security funding as part of a $1.7 million grocery-support initiative included in the city's 2026 budget earlier this week. "Keeping our neighborhood grocery stores safe and supported is essential to making sure every Seattleite has a reliable, affordable grocery store near them," Wilson said on social media Monday. The plan will help 10 independent grocery stores pay for improvements and get a year of business support, while stores hit hard by retail theft can get one-time funding for security upgrades and repairs. 'WASTEFUL DISTRACTION': EXPERTS SLAM MAMDANI'S TAXPAYER-FUNDED GROCERY STORES The security funding is already drawing criticism from conservatives who argue the city is spending public money to help businesses absorb the consequences of crime rather than focusing enough resources on preventing it. "The best way to support grocery store — and all businesses — is to actually enforce the law with a fully staffed and funded police department. Giving money or resources to fix businesses that are broken by crime is a bandage on a bullet wound," Seattle-based KTTH host and conservative commentator Jason Rantz told Fox News Digital. SMALL-BUSINESS OWNER URGES SEATTLE LEADERS TO ACT NOW ON PUBLIC DRUG USE AND SLOW EMERGENCY RESPONSE "We don’t need to think outside the box here. Just enforce the law and put criminals in jail. That works like a charm and will save everyone money and headaches," Rantz added. "Is there no single human in Seattle willing to identify the criminals and end the crime instead," asked an X user. "Seattle is arguably the worst city in the entire country right now, in terms of the rampant crime, widespread degradation and lawlessness that’s apparently gotten exponentially worse across the board over the last 2-3 yrs," another user chimed in. NEW YORK SOCIALIST LAWMAKER TAKES HEAT AFTER SAYING SHOPLIFTING RESULTS FROM 'BIOLOGICAL NEED' "That used to be called the police department. What are these security guards going to do? Make arrests? Observe & report? The criminals will walk right past the security with their stolen goods. If they detain they will be sued. Cops will not arrest the shoplifters or prosecute," said one person. "Goodness! imagine how much nicer the city would be if they simply arrested and charged criminals and put them in jail? Normal people shouldn't have to shop at stores with security guards. NONE of this was necessary in most parts of Seattle 15 years ago," wrote an X user. "So we are working around the problem by increasing security instead of arresting the problem," said another person. The city will also work with the Independent Grocers Alliance to study eight neighborhoods for potential new grocery stores, according to the plan. Wilson floated the idea of exploring a "public option" for grocery stores during her 2025 mayoral campaign, including models that could involve publicly supported or city-run grocery stores. While the new initiative is separate from those proposals, critics argued the city should focus more heavily on arresting and prosecuting retail thieves rather than spending additional money helping stores deal with the damage caused by crime. The grocery security funding was first proposed by former Mayor Bruce Harrell as $1 million for grocery-store security in his 2026 budget, specifically targeting retail theft, property damage and other crimes. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP City leaders pushed to cut police spending amid the 2020 "Black Lives Matter" movement and the city subsequently experienced a steep decline in police staffing, with the department falling from 1,424 officers in 2019 to 1,054 in 2024 before hiring began to rebound, the Seattle Mayor's Office previously reported. The broader theft problem remains significant in Seattle, where police recorded nearly 7,500 larceny-theft offenses across the city's five precincts through May, making it the most commonly reported crime category in every precinct. Fox News Digital reached out to the mayor's office on Tuesday.

articles.title: Lost in translation: Israel, Huckabee blast Macron over Hamas comments as France clarifies wording
articles.summary: President Donald Trump vowed Iran will never have a nuclear weapon as United Nations leaders accused Israel of war crimes and forced displacement.
articles.body: President Donald Trump offered a roaring counterbalance to a spate of world leaders bashing Israel or appearing to equivocate between the Oct. 7 Hamas terror attacks and Jerusalem’s response — as one world leader was assailed for his comments on Hamas. Gaza dominated the opening day of the U.N. General Assembly on Tuesday, despite a ceasefire, as world leaders accused Israel of continuing to displace Palestinians and undermine prospects for peace. French President Emmanuel Macron accused Israel of violating Palestinian rights in the West Bank, questioning the justification for its actions and making a remark that was translated as "Hamas was never active in the West Bank." MIDDLE EAST TAKES CENTER STAGE AT UN AS REGIONAL LEADERS CONFRONT IRAN WAR, GAZA AND HOUTHI THREAT Israeli U.N. Ambassador Danny Danon challenged his claim about Hamas’ presence in the West Bank. "French President Emmanuel Macron claimed from the UN podium that Hamas has ‘never been active’ in Judea and Samaria. Just two days ago, a French citizen was murdered there," Danon wrote on X. "Mr. President, Emmanuel Macron, do your homework before lecturing Israel. Check the facts." Asked by Fox News Digital to clarify Macron’s remarks, a French Foreign Ministry spokesperson said: "The president meant to say that Hamas does not govern the West Bank. His remarks should therefore not be misinterpreted." In response to the comments, U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee reposted Israel's Minister of Diaspora and Combating Antisemitism. Huckabee stated, "Hard to imagine a more out of touch with reality speech than Macron at UN. @AmichaiChikli corrects the record. Hamas is an evil scourge, and they have killed innocent American citizens. Chickli's post noted in part that, "Since 1990, Hamas has carried out more than 80 lethal terrorist attacks originating in or directed from Judea and Samaria, murdering more than 350 Israeli civilians." Judea and Samaria is another term used for the West Bank. Macron also accused Israel of violating Palestinian rights in the West Bank and undermining the sovereignty of neighboring Lebanon, where he said villages in the south were being "razed." Macron questioned the credibility of the international community’s recognition of Palestinian statehood if it failed to act on the situation in Gaza. "Some claim that peace has been achieved," he said, calling the situation "shameful." U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres, in his final address to the U.N. General Assembly (UNGA) as secretary-general, opened fire on Israel’s response in Gaza, describing it as "a scale of killing and destruction unlike anything I have witnessed in all my years as Secretary-General." "Amid the turmoil engulfing the region, we must not lose sight of the devastating situation in the Occupied Palestinian Territory," he said, as the world approaches three years since the Hamas terror attacks that sparked the Israeli military response he spent much of his speech criticizing. At the same time, Guterres lamented the ongoing conflict in Sudan, saying the war-torn East African nation is a place the "world looks away" from wrongly. Yet his decision to single out Gaza as "the worst" devastation he had witnessed during his tenure raised questions about the international community's uneven attention to two of the world's deadliest conflicts. Approximately 72,000 Palestinians have been reported killed in Gaza, according to the Hamas-run Health Ministry, compared with an estimated 150,000 people killed in Sudan's civil war. Many of those killed in Gaza include terrorists. King Abdullah II of Jordan, a regional U.S. ally whose country signed a peace agreement with Israel in 1994, doubled down on the anti-Israel tenor, accusing Jerusalem of "war crimes." "In my region, from Lebanon to Yemen, to Sudan, protracted conflict is deepening humanitarian suffering," Abdullah said. "And if anyone had any doubt that a crisis in our part of the world stays there, just look at the energy and grocery bills of ordinary families, from Mumbai to Madrid to Minnesota." WORLD LEADERS DESCEND ON NEW YORK FOR UNGA — BUT WHO REALLY HAS AMERICA’S EAR? Abdullah said Jordanian field hospitals had been targeted during the first 300 days of the "so-called ceasefire" and lamented the deaths of Palestinian children. He also praised Trump for "pushing hard for peace" while pivoting to fault Israel for "moving the goalposts" and allegedly destroying civilian infrastructure in Gaza. "The question is, is this the behavior of a democratic state governed by law? What is unfolding across the West Bank is not a series of isolated acts. It is elements of a single policy to compel an entire population to leave their land," Abdullah said. "And there is a name for that: forced displacement. And that is a war crime." Abdullah also accused Israel of harboring territorial ambitions in Syria, calling on the international community to act. Just before Abdullah, President Donald Trump offered a scathing counterweight to the invective directed at the Netanyahu administration and Israel’s response to Palestinian terrorism. BRITAIN’S DRAMATIC CRACKDOWN ON ISRAELI SETTLEMENTS SPARKS FIERCE RESPONSE AS US BLOWBACK LOOMS "Iran will never have a nuclear weapon" was a mantra repeated by Trump from the dais, as he noted that the Khamenei regime had also celebrated Oct. 7 as a "service to humanity" while murdering thousands of Iranian citizens in recent months, according to the president. "Just imagine such a vile regime, wherever empowered to carry out large-scale terror attacks from behind a nuclear shield. This was the reality we had to confront, the reality that far too many preferred to ignore," he said, taking occasional swipes at nations — and previous U.S. leaders — who refused to help neutralize the Iranian threat. "Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?" he asked. "But I believe we’ll make a deal right after the election," he added, suggesting Iran is waiting to see whether Republicans retain control of Congress while noting that he himself is not on the ballot. Meanwhile, criticism of Israel continued from the dais throughout the day. Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva said that former Israeli Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin and former Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat were "statesmen" who sought solutions with courage and clarity. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER "They were defeated by hatred," Lula da Silva claimed, according to the U.N.’s transcript of his remarks. "Generations of Palestinians will carry the pain and trauma left by the genocide of women and children perpetrated by Netanyahu[‘s] government in Gaza," he said. Danon told Fox News Digital that, "Unfortunately, it’s not new, but the U.N. is obsessed with Israel." "Instead of focusing and dealing with the real issues, they all gather and gang against Israel," he said. "[It is] the weakness of the secretary general. That is why we are grateful for President Trump, who came to the U.N., delivered a very powerful speech with moral clarity, but we are used to it… Unfortunately, instead of taking practical actions to improve the world, it's much easier to blame Israel about everything," he said. Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, called Gaza "the world's biggest graveyard for children" and compared the situation there to Holocaust-era concentration camps, continuing his history of comparing Israel to Nazi Germany. Danon said it is legitimate to criticize Israel and that its leaders welcome debate — but that the U.N. instead delved into "pure hate [and] incitement," singling out Erdoğan, who is supposed to be a Western ally. "[He] comes here every year, compares the Israelis to the Nazis. That's shameful. That's shameful. And he shows that he's an antisemite. He doesn't really care about the Palestinians. He just wants to sow chaos and instigate against the Jewish people." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP As for King Abdullah's remarks, Danon said, "He should know better. We work with Jordan, we support Jordan, we defended Jordan in the past. But unfortunately, many leaders, when they come here, they don't speak about the cooperation with Israel, the economical or security cooperation. They join the group and they always criticize us." Fox News Digital's Hannah Brennan contributed to this report.

articles.title: CNN, Politico and MS NOW to face off with Trump administration in court over White House ban
articles.summary: The news outlets that President Donald Trump abruptly banned from accessing the White House will be in court Wednesday to argue the policy is unconstitutional.
articles.body: The trio of media outlets that President Donald Trump abruptly banned from accessing the White House will be in court Wednesday to argue their expulsion was unconstitutional and should be lifted immediately. “This ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles,” lawyers for CNN, Politico and MS NOW said in a court filing Monday ahead of the hearing. “The ban is unconstitutional and should be immediately restrained,” they contended, citing legal precedent in the District of Columbia and U.S. Supreme Court. The news organizations are scheduled to make their case to U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly at a 3:30 p.m. ET hearing. Late Tuesday, the Justice Department defended the ban in a court filing, arguing that Trump had decided the outlets “failed to maintain basic minimum ‘standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House Complex, including’ by ‘publishing sensitive or classified information.’” The outlets’ “access to the White House is a privilege — not a right,” the filing said. On Tuesday, the White House Press Office sent letters to the three outlets alleging their coverage involved “trafficking in verifiable falsehoods about national security and other issues, and publishing sensitive or classified information,” the department said in the filing. The letters also were filed in court. The articles cited in the letters included reporting on the construction of the White House ballroom and its related military security complex, the status of munitions supplies being used in the Iran war, an alleged FBI leak investigation involving a journalist, and sanctions on Russia. In the letters, the administration gave the organizations a deadline of 5 p.m. Friday to “contest this initial decision” to bar them from the White House or the decision “will be final,” the filing said. The outlets did not immediately respond to NBC News’ requests for comment on the allegations in the filing. Kelly was nominated to the bench by Trump in his first term but ruled against him in a similar case back in 2018, when the White House pulled press credentials from then-CNN reporter Jim Acosta. In a post on Truth Social on Monday, Trump said Kelly is a “great judge” for the media outlets, and suggested he believes he’ll rule against his administration. “[A]s usual, we’ll go for appeal,” he wrote, “because Fake News people and publications that only write negatively” should not be “allowed access to the most important Office anywhere in the World.” Trump also criticized the judge as “totally disloyal” in a separate post late Tuesday. The three news organizations have pointed to similar remarks by Trump as proof they’re victims of impermissible “viewpoint discrimination.” Trump announced the outlets’ ban from the White House in a Truth Social post Friday, and said it was “a result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!” “Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow,” he added. Responding to questions from a reporter in the Oval Office a short time later, Trump referred to it as “the ban on the free press.” “Very simple ban. I don’t want them in my office. I don’t want them here,” he said. He said the policy was in response to “cumulative stories over the last few years.” “They purposely write negative news. And they do that because they want to try and diminish the Republicans and a Republican administration,” he said. “If they could straighten themselves out, I’d love it,” he added. The outlets’ suit said Trump’s “words leave no doubt that banning Plaintiffs from the White House is retaliation for their protected newsgathering and speech — retaliation that is intended to cow them into changing their reporting and threaten other journalists lest they suffer the same fate. That is a paradigmatic First Amendment violation” and “flatly unconstitutional.” The ban has already impacted news coverage, the suit says. CNN is a member of the five-network rotation “for the primary television pool (also called the network pool) and absorbs 20% of the costs associated with such coverage,” the suit says. The pool covers “events and locations where there is limited physical space for journalists,” their court papers say, and for “most of what the President does each day, the pool is the only source of independent reporting, video, and photographs available to the press and the public.” “When CNN is the designated network pooler, CNN’s crew supplies the video and audio of the events involving the President and other White House officials to the other four networks and, through them and through pool distribution arrangements, to news organizations and the public. Among the recipients of the pool material are the more than 1,000 local affiliate television stations across the United States that receive the pool feed through CNN.” NBC, ABC, CBS and Fox News are the other members of the rotation. MS NOW is a rotating member of the secondary pool, while Politico is a member of the rotating print pool. CNN had been scheduled to be the pool camera Monday, and the other networks in the TV network pool jointly declined to step in and replace its coverage, resulting in Trump’s remarks at a ribbon-cutting ceremony at the White House being inaudible. His remarks at the United Nations on Tuesday and alongside New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani at a press conference Monday were picked up by U.N. cameras and local news outlets, respectively. Trump defended the bans in a social media statement Monday and added a new argument — that “fake news” is a national security issue. “The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish. It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America,” he wrote. “It is a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!”

articles.title: Pro-life leader sounds alarm after doctor gets 6 months for forcing abortion pills on girlfriend
articles.summary: Marjorie Dannenfelser slams the six-month sentence for Hassan-James Abbas, who forced crushed abortion pills into his pregnant girlfriend's mouth.
articles.body: Marjorie Dannenfelser, the president of SBA Pro-Life America, told Fox News Digital that U.S. law has not caught up with the growing availability of abortion medication, allowing predators who use the drugs to end pregnancies without women’s consent to face relatively light consequences. She pointed to the case of Hassan-James Abbas, an Ohio man accused of forcing abortion pills into his pregnant girlfriend's mouth in December 2024. He was sentenced earlier this month to six months in prison. The woman, Jona Affholder, went to the hospital and ultimately lost the baby. "The fact that this guy got only six months in prison for his crime says a lot about the state of our culture right now," Dannenfelser said. "This was a very much wanted pregnancy. She could support the baby on her own and didn't need his help. But he had other ideas in mind." PRO-LIFE CEO PREDICTS TRUMP FDA NOMINEE COULD BRING RENEWED SCRUTINY TO ABORTION DRUG RISKS Abbas, then a surgical resident at the University of Toledo, began dating Affholder in early October 2024, according to a lawsuit she filed against him. Sometime in December that year, Affholder got pregnant. Authorities said once he found out, he illegally obtained mifepristone and misoprostol using his estranged wife's identification information. It is unclear whether Abbas prescribed the drugs himself. Taken together, the two medications terminate early pregnancies: mifepristone blocks progesterone, a hormone needed to sustain the pregnancy, while misoprostol causes contractions that expel the fetus. TRUMP-BACKED VIVEK RAMASWAMY WINS OHIO GOP GUBERNATORIAL PRIMARY, WILL FACE DEMOCRAT AMY ACTON Under current FDA rules, patients do not have to see a physician in person to receive a prescription, allowing mifepristone to be prescribed after a telehealth visit and mailed by a certified pharmacy. After getting his hands on the pills, he began offering Affholder hot chocolate and tea, "which was out of character for their relationship," according to the Lucas County Prosecutor's Office. On Dec. 18, 2024, Abbas invited her to his home in Holland, Ohio. Prosecutors said despite being aware of Affholder's intention to keep the baby, he climbed on top of her in bed, held her down and shoved crushed abortion pills into her mouth. Court records show that when Affholder tried to call 911, he took the phone out of her hand and hung it up. Eventually, she was able to leave Abbas's residence and get to the hospital. Affholder described this experience in a Daily Wire op-ed published in June 2026. HAWLEY SENDS CRIMINAL REFERRAL OF 'LEFT-WING DARK-MONEY' GROUP OVER MAILED ABORTION DRUGS "I fought him off and ran to call 911. He took my cell and my keys, blocking me from leaving. I rushed to the kitchen, trying to rinse the powder from my mouth. But he continued to restrain me, buying each minute for the drugs to do their intended purpose of killing our kid," Affholder wrote. "When he assumed the drugs had sufficiently aborted our baby, he returned my belongings, and I went straight to the hospital," she added. According to Affholder's account, she began hemorrhaging after arriving at the hospital and ultimately miscarried. Abbas, who was arrested the next day, initially pleaded not guilty. In May 2026, he pleaded no contest to four felony charges: disrupting public services, unlawfully distributing abortion-inducing drugs, identity fraud and using deception to obtain a dangerous drug. As part of the plea agreement, prosecutors dropped charges of abduction and tampering with evidence. The state had alleged that Abbas drove away from the home on the night of the assault and threw the remaining pills out his car window. BLUE STATE SHIELD LAWS ALLOWED 330K ABORTION PILLS TO BE SENT TO ABORTION BAN STATES, PRO-LIFE GROUP FINDS Dannenfelser contrasted Abbas' six-month sentence with Ohio's penalties for rape, which can carry years or even life in prison depending on the circumstances. "But... this coercion and this attack that led to the death of her wanted child gets only six months," she said. In February 2024, Mason Herring, of Texas, received the exact same sentence — six months — for slipping misoprostol into his then wife's drinks. The baby survived but initially faced severe developmental delays. "If you are Amy Acton running for governor [of Ohio], if you are Sherrod Brown running for the Senate, you need to answer for this because their Republican opponents are very much for limiting these drugs or controlling them at least," Dannenfelser added. Fox News Digital reached out to both campaigns for comment. Dannenfelser also criticized Planned Parenthood and pro-choice advocates, accusing them of failing to speak out about Affholder’s case and others like it. "Where are the advocates, the feminists, the people who are against the coercion of women, the people who are 'my body, my choice,' the people who say that medical care is all that they're really looking for," she said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Planned Parenthood does not appear to have publicly commented on Affholder's case, but the organization has explicitly condemned the act of giving women abortion drugs without their knowledge or consent. Fox News Digital reached out to Planned Parenthood for comment. Dannenfelser said the Department of Justice should take a more active role in prosecuting cases involving forced abortions. "We do have every hope that the attorney general will move on this, and he's referenced it at the Dallas convention that people who are pushing death in a pill will be disappointed," she said. "That is the surest way to justice." On Tuesday, Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, joined Dannenfelser in demanding Attorney General Todd Blanche take action, referencing Affholder's case. "My constituent was held down and force-fed crushed-up mail-order abortion pills," Moreno wrote to Blanche. "Unsurprisingly, reckless Biden-era mail-in abortion policies are responsible for this hell-on-earth tragedy."

articles.title: Ayuntamiento y Ministerio de Vivienda se acusan mutuamente por el desahucio de Maricarmen: "El Ministerio miente"
articles.standfirst: El caso de la mujer de 87 años obligada a abandonar su casa enfrenta a ambas adminsitraciones
articles.summary: El caso de la mujer de 87 años obligada a abandonar su casa enfrenta a ambas adminsitraciones
articles.body: El desahucio de Maricarmen, la mujer de 87 años que ha vivido 70 años en su casa del distrito madrileño de Retiro, ha provocado un enfrentamiento entre el Ayuntamiento de Madrid y el Ministerio de Vivienda. El lanzamiento se ejecutó este miércoles, después de varios intentos y pese a las peticiones para buscar una solución. El Ministerio, dirigido por Isabel Rodríguez, reclamó al Ayuntamiento y a la Comunidad de Madrid que intervinieran y cuestionó que el Consistorio hubiera acreditado la situación de vulnerabilidad de la anciana. También respaldó el requerimiento de Naciones Unidas para suspender cautelarmente el desalojo y aseguró haber intentado mediar con la propiedad. Así mismo, Rodríguez ha confirmado esta mañana de miércoles, 23 de septiembre, en el Congreso que se pusieron en contacto con la empresa propietaria de esta casa “para hacerles entender que por encima de su interés económico está el carácter social de esta vivienda y la vida de Maricarmen”. La respuesta municipal fue tajante. Fuentes del Ayuntamiento acusaron al Ministerio de faltar a la verdad: "El Ministerio de Vivienda miente". Según el Consistorio, los servicios sociales emitieron el informe de vulnerabilidad en octubre de 2025, a petición del juzgado, y mantienen desde entonces un seguimiento de Maricarmen. El alcalde, José Luis Martínez-Almeida, insistió en esa versión y pidió a la ministra que "no mienta" ni genere "enfrentamientos inútiles". El Ayuntamiento sostiene que ofreció a la mujer recursos de alojamiento anteriormente, pero que ella rechazó las plazas propuestas. Entre las prestaciones municipales figuran también ayuda a domicilio. El conflicto incluye otra discrepancia: el Ayuntamiento afirma haber ofrecido alternativas asistenciales, mientras que Maricarmen y el Sindicato de Inquilinas sostienen que las opciones no constituían una solución. El colectivo denunció que una de las propuestas era una residencia privada de más de 1.200 euros mensuales, una cantidad difícil de asumir con su pensión. Mientras las administraciones intercambiaban reproches, el Ministerio defendía que el Gobierno había trabajado para encontrar una salida y señalaba que la propiedad rechazó negociar. El Ejecutivo también ha planteado un decreto para casos de personas vulnerables. Por su parte, Mónica García, ministra de Sanidad y portavoz de Más Madrid, insta al PSOE a llevar el Real Decreto Ley de Vivienda al próximo Consejo de Ministros “sí o sí” porque el partido socialista “no puede seguir dilatándolo más, ni PP, Junts y Vox pueden volver a votar en contra”, ha escrito en su perfil de X. Finalmente, Maricarmen fue desalojada y trasladada en camilla al Hospital Gregorio Marañón. El Ayuntamiento anunció que Samur Social le ofrecería un recurso habitacional de emergencia tras el lanzamiento.
